item.title: Hackers pile on PHP2Shell as AWS reveals attacks began before disclosure
item.description: Attackers are hammering servers with millions of attempts to exploit the critical PHP2Shell vulnerabilities , with Amazon revealing that someone was already going after the flaws four days before they were publicly disclosed. Cloudflare says it has recorded a staggering increase in attacks targeting the two vulnerabilities, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, since details began circulating earlier this week. According to Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince , the company spotted thousands of exploitation attempts in the 10 hours before the vulnerabilities were publicly announced. That figure jumped to tens of thousands within 45 minutes of disclosure, hundreds of thousands within two hours, and has since climbed into the millions. And the attackers aren't simply recycling the same exploit. Cloudflare said it has seen miscreants tweaking their payloads in an attempt to sneak past its web application firewall (WAF) protections, apparently using feedback from blocked requests to work out what might get through. Security outfit Hadrian also sounded the alarm on October 21, reporting that PHP2Shell was being "exploited in the wild at scale." "Most of the attacks we observe abuse PHP's session upload-progress path, and we expect more exploit paths to appear before and after the fix ships," the company warned. More worrying, some attackers appear to have started before the vulnerabilities were even public knowledge. Amazon Threat Intelligence says it detected an attempt to exploit PHP2Shell on October 17, four days before patches were released. The activity was picked up by MadPot, Amazon's network of honeypots designed to lure attackers and record what they get up to. "While the vulnerability was under embargo, the targeting of a honeypot from an anonymized IP address suggests the activity was conducted by a threat actor, though it remains unclear how the actor acquired exploit information prior to disclosure," Amazon said. The retail and cloud giant said it detected multiple proof-of-concept exploits on October 21, with the earliest appearing around 0200 UTC, some 12 hours before the patches were released. Over the following six hours, further attempts arrived from different anonymized infrastructure, using a variety of payloads. Amazon reckons this points to multiple attackers rather than a single group. Whether any of those attempts would have worked against real-world systems remains unclear. The findings add another layer to an already messy disclosure. As The Register reported on Wednesday , the PHP Foundation has accused supply-chain security vendor Chainguard of putting websites at risk by publishing patched PHP builds before the agreed disclosure deadline. However, Amazon's October 17 detection suggests at least one cybercrim was already trying to exploit the bugs days before that incident. The vulnerabilities themselves are particularly nasty. "Most of the attacks we observe abuse PHP's session upload-progress path, and we expect more exploit paths to appear before and after the fix ships," the company warned. Amazon Threat Intelligence says it detected an attempt to exploit PHP2Shell on October 17, four days before patches were released. The activity was picked up by MadPot, Amazon's network of honeypots designed to lure attackers and record what they get up to. "While the vulnerability was under embargo, the targeting of a honeypot from an anonymized IP address suggests the activity was conducted by a threat actor, though it remains unclear how the actor acquired exploit information prior to disclosure," Amazon said. The retail and cloud giant said it detected multiple proof-of-concept exploits on October 21, with the earliest appearing around 0200 UTC, some 12 hours before the patches were released. Over the following six hours, further attempts arrived from different anonymized infrastructure, using a variety of payloads. Amazon reckons this points to multiple attackers rather than a single group. Whether any of those attempts would have worked against real-world systems remains unclear. The findings add another layer to an already messy disclosure. As The Register reported on Wednesday , the PHP Foundation has accused supply-chain security vendor Chainguard of putting websites at risk by publishing patched PHP builds before the agreed disclosure deadline. However, Amazon's October 17 detection suggests at least one cybercrim was already trying to exploit the bugs days before that incident. The vulnerabilities themselves are particularly nasty. Both carry a critical 9.2 severity rating and affect PHP's handling of memory, potentially allowing unauthenticated attackers to execute malicious code on vulnerable servers. Unlike flaws in individual plugins or applications, these bugs affect the PHP runtime itself, putting a potentially enormous number of websites at risk regardless of which content management system they use. Cloudflare says it has deployed WAF protections across its free and paid plans, although it has stressed that these are no substitute for patching. With attackers already trying their luck before the fixes were available, admins may have more than just a patching backlog to worry about. Amazon is advising organizations to investigate suspicious activity dating back to at least October 17, rather than assuming their systems were safe until the vulnerabilities became public. ®

item.title: How tech became the villain of the US midterms
item.description: Datacenters, AI and distaste for the billionaires developing it has soured Americans on big tech How will Trump’s mass deportation agenda shape the US midterm elections? Our reporters answer your questions The campaign ad begins with a clear, idyllic stream that suddenly turns sludge-brown as two concrete datacenters slam on to its banks. Another facility thuds down on a peaceful suburban park, and two more crush-green pastures as an ominous soundtrack to a disaster movie blares. “They’re coming for our rivers. Our neighborhoods. Our farmland,” a deep-voiced narrator says. “Because Brent Taylor wrote the law allowing datacenters to take over Tennessee.” Continue reading...

Our reporters answer your questions The campaign ad begins with a clear, idyllic stream that suddenly turns sludge-brown as two concrete datacenters slam on to its banks. Another facility thuds down on a peaceful suburban park, and two more crush-green pastures as an ominous soundtrack to a disaster movie blares. “They’re coming for our rivers. Our neighborhoods. Our farmland,” a deep-voiced narrator says. “Because Brent Taylor wrote the law allowing datacenters to take over Tennessee.” Continue reading...

item.title: 333 Tor exit nodes hijacked to intercept SSH traffic and retrieve plaintext email
item.description: Unknown hackers hijacked more than 300 Tor exit nodes and reconfigured them to favor unencrypted email traffic and redirect SSH connections through servers they controlled, a researcher reported Tuesday. The hijacking began in late August, when, according to Tor volunteers , the attacker used a valid password that had been reused to gain access to a Tor management server. The attacker then installed Ebury , a backdoor written for Linux that was discovered 12 years ago. Mysteries remain Then the attacker connected from the management server to a second Tor server, called Switzerland2, through SSH, using an RSA key that, for unknown reasons, investigators couldn’t find among Switzerland2’s authorized keys. With administrative control of Switzerland2, the attackers installed Ebury there as well. Finally, the attacker reconfigured settings on two exit nodes that Switzerland2 hosted. Read full article Comments

item.title: Microsoft says ConnectWise breach let Chinese spies loose on 2,250 cloud tenants
item.description: China-aligned attackers used AI agents and compromised ConnectWise application credentials to target more than 2,250 Microsoft 365 tenants, Microsoft says. The Windows giant revealed this week that the attackers, tracked as Storm-0940, used an open source AI penetration-testing tool called ARTEX to automate attacks against Microsoft 365 environments. In some cases, they went from picking a target to gaining privileged cloud access in less than three hours. The findings shed more light on the ConnectWise security incident , which saw the IT management vendor pull the plug on its Cloud Backup, SaaS Security, and Cloud Management services after discovering unauthorized access to application identities. ConnectWise didn't initially identify who was responsible, but Microsoft has now pointed the finger at Storm-0940, a China-linked espionage crew that's been operating since at least 2021. The group has traditionally relied on the usual tricks, including password spraying and exploiting internet-facing applications, but this time it used AI to do some of the heavy lifting. ARTEX is an open source penetration-testing framework written in Go that uses AI agents to automate everything from reconnaissance and vulnerability discovery to credential attacks and data theft. Microsoft says Storm-0940 began using it as early as September to target organizations worldwide, including government agencies, defense contractors, banks, manufacturers, and tech firms. Between October 10 and 14, the hackers made more than 151,000 failed sign-in attempts against 327 accounts at eight organizations. Microsoft observed no successful logins from that password-spraying campaign, but then the attackers shifted to compromised ConnectWise application identities. The compromised application credentials let the attackers exploit permissions customers had already granted to ConnectWise services, without needing an interactive user login. Armed with ARTEX, Storm-0940 attempted to authenticate against more than 2,250 Microsoft 365 tenants, at times reaching 2,900 attempts a minute. Microsoft also observed AI-accelerated activity through Microsoft Graph, including reconnaissance, application credential changes, and attempts to modify privileges, potentially allowing the attackers to stick around even after the original credentials were revoked. Most attempts failed, though Microsoft says the hackers still managed to establish persistent privileged access at numerous organizations. It hasn't disclosed how many customers were compromised or whether any data was stolen, cautioning that a successful login doesn't necessarily mean information was accessed. ConnectWise CEO Manny Rivelo said the company had contained the affected application connections and was gradually restoring services, although shutting down those connections wouldn't necessarily boot out attackers who had already established a foothold in customer environments. ConnectWise has been here before. In May 2025, it admitted

Microsoft says it has spotted attackers from several geographic regions using the framework, which is freely available for penetration testing. The underlying techniques are nothing new – stolen credentials, password spraying, and application abuse – but Microsoft says AI helped Storm-0940 execute them faster, with some attacks progressing from initial targeting to privileged cloud access in under three hours. ®

item.title: ‘Pure arrogance’: anger in Finland as Google illegally fells 250,000 trees for datacentre
item.description: Company ordered to stop work at two sites in country, which has found itself at forefront of tech firms’ latest push Behind a wire fence lies a vast gaping wound of earth. Before Google’s arrival a few months ago, an estimated quarter of a million trees occupied the 330 hectares (815 acres) of forest near the town of Muhos in rural northern Finland. Now they are all gone. After the tech company illegally stripped the entire area to build a datacentre – taking even the top soil with it – all that remains is a vast expanse of mud indented with the trail marks of machinery, puddles and mounds of earth, roots and branches. Residents say that brown water flowing off the site is going into a stream that feeds the Oulujoki River. Continue reading...

item.title: UN says we're going to blow past 1.5º warming, offers a "now what?" answer
item.description: In 2015, all but two countries agreed to make an effort to keep global temperatures from reaching 1.5° C above pre-industrial readings. Since then, most of the world has largely treated what they signed on to as aspirational, and one of the largest emitters (the US) has alternately withdrawn and recommitted to the agreement. Meanwhile, the planet has responded as expected to steadily rising carbon emissions and appears to be practically at the 1.5° limit. On Wednesday, for the first time, the United Nations Environmental Programme (UNEP) acknowledged that reality and conceded that the goal of keeping warming below 1.5° was no longer a viable one. Instead, its new goalposts focus on keeping both how long we exceed that limit and how much we exceed it by, at a minimum. Doing that will require both dramatic emissions cuts now and the removal of hundreds of gigatonnes of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere before the century is out. Bowing to the inevitable Depending on which baseline you use to establish pre-industrial temperatures, as well as which reconstruction of global temperatures you rely on, the world has either gotten very close to, or already exceeded, the 1.5° milestone. The current El Niño event, which appears exceptionally strong, will almost certainly mean that we've gone over it no matter which records you choose. Read full article Comments

item.title: Veteran ESA probe rolls out welcome mat for Japan's Phobos mission
item.description: Japan's mission to the Martian moon Phobos launched this week, with a veteran European probe expected to be waiting when it arrives. JAXA, Japan's space agency, confirmed that the Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) spacecraft launched aboard an H3 rocket on October 19 at 19:41 UTC – October 20 in Japan. On October 21, it said that initial critical operations, including solar array deployment, were complete. Equipment checks will follow as the spacecraft prepares for its outbound cruise. The probe is due to reach Mars in 2027, deploy the Idefix rover on Phobos, and attempt one or two landings on the moon itself. The rover is named after the dog from the Asterix comics. Scientists plan to collect about 10 g of material from Phobos and send it to Earth, with a return planned for 2031. The European Space Agency (ESA) is supporting the trip with Mars Express (MEX), which has orbited Mars since 2003. A former team member told The Register that plans include joint observations and imaging of MMX's landing site. MEX's latest mission extension runs to 2029, covering MMX's expected arrival. The former team member described it as definitely the last – before adding that "the first 'last ever extension' was in about 2007." Discussions about another "last ever extension" could begin in 2028 or 2029, with support for MMX and the Rosalind Franklin rover among the potential reasons to keep MEX going. Funding and scientific returns would determine the outcome. A software update announced in May 2025 reduced wear on its gyroscopes, potentially allowing them to last until 2034. Rosalind Franklin is due for launch in 2028 after repeated delays and Russia's ejection from the project. MEX will likely be able to image the rover's landing site on the surface of Mars and take part in data relay operations, though ESA's Trace Gas Orbiter (TGO) will be the main relay asset. Several years ago, another team member joked that MEX was so tough it would punch straight through Phobos if sent there for disposal. We wouldn't take that as an engineering assessment, but it says something about the team's affection for their spacecraft. MEX's longevity is a tribute to its builders and operators. With funding through 2029, it could welcome MMX next year. Further extensions might keep it working through the sample-return departure and Rosalind Franklin's arrival. "We all want our '30 years in flight' T-shirts," the former team member said. ®

item.title: IT department and auditors at major pharmacy chain got into a rip-roaring fight about using 'password' on Cisco firewall
item.description: Welcome back to PWNED, the column where we talk about companies and organizations that leave the doors wide open to attackers. This week’s sad story involves a major American pharmacy chain that couldn’t fill a prescription for password security. Have a story about someone leaving a gaping hole in their network? Share it with us at pwned@sitpub.com . Anonymity is available upon request. Our tale comes courtesy of red team and pen testing specialist Dahvid Schloss, who currently serves as COO of Suzu Labs , a cybersecurity company that boasts “we break your systems before adversaries do.” Over a career spanning more than 15 years, Schloss has assessed the security of numerous businesses, including a large US pharmacy retailer that he asked us not to name. He wasn’t asked to break in, just to do an audit on all of the org’s corporate switches, routers, and firewalls. “So, I come across this firewall,” Schloss said. “That is an edge firewall, meaning this is what touches the internet. This part will add its enable password, which is the term Cisco uses for administrator. It had the enable password as 'password.' Just p-a-s-s-w-o-r-d.” As Schloss noted, the enable command on Cisco devices allows the user to gain administrative rights to the firewall, controlling network traffic. If someone connected to that firewall, either via SSH or through an exploit, and got normal user privileges, they could then elevate those privileges to admin and do something like shut off all traffic from the intranet to the outside world. Schloss actually didn’t guess that the password was “password,” but instead was able to decrypt the file holding the passwords by breaking Cisco’s own protection, something he said is easy to do. “That enable password was stored as Cisco IOS type 7, which isn’t really a hash,” he said. “It’s more of a reversible encoding with a publicly known key. Even back then, it was best practice not to use it.” But even if the password were stored in a secure place, it would be very easy for a threat actor to guess. So he marked the password failure down as a “high find,” a bad type of vuln that needs to be fixed right away. When he brought the password to the company’s auditing department, they put him on a phone call with the auditing team, the entire IT team, his own manager, and others. On the packed call, the auditing team, who had commissioned Schloss’s work, was very concerned about the firewall password, but the IT team didn’t think it was a very serious problem. The two sides screamed at each other for more than an hour while Schloss and his colleagues sat there quietly, staring at their cameras. “The audit team is like ‘yeah, we gotta fix this.’ And the directors were really harping on ‘this needs to be done’ and the IT team starts firing back,” Schloss explained. “It’s like ‘Why? Who’s gonna? What does it matter? No, this isn’t a high-priority find. This is maybe a medium. Yeah, it’s bad, but it’s not that bad.’” The call dragged on so lon

item.content:encoded: Welcome back to PWNED, the column where we talk about companies and organizations that leave the doors wide open to attackers. This week’s sad story involves a major American pharmacy chain that couldn’t fill a prescription for password security. Have a story about someone leaving a gaping hole in their network? Share it with us at pwned@sitpub.com . Anonymity is available upon request. This part will add its enable password, which is the term Cisco uses for administrator. It had the enable password as 'password.' Just p-a-s-s-w-o-r-d.” As Schloss noted, the enable command on Cisco devices allows the user to gain administrative rights to the firewall, controlling network traffic. If someone connected to that firewall, either via SSH or through an exploit, and got normal user privileges, they could then elevate those privileges to admin and do something like shut off all traffic from the intranet to the outside world. Schloss actually didn’t guess that the password was “password,” but instead was able to decrypt the file holding the passwords by breaking Cisco’s own protection, something he said is easy to do. “That enable password was stored as Cisco IOS type 7, which isn’t really a hash,” he said. “It’s more of a reversible encoding with a publicly known key. Even back then, it was best practice not to use it.” But even if the password were stored in a secure place, it would be very easy for a threat actor to guess. So he marked the password failure down as a “high find,” a bad type of vuln that needs to be fixed right away. When he brought the password to the company’s auditing department, they put him on a phone call with the auditing team, the entire IT team, his own manager, and others. On the packed call, the auditing team, who had commissioned Schloss’s work, was very concerned about the firewall password, but the IT team didn’t think it was a very serious problem. The two sides screamed at each other for more than an hour while Schloss and his colleagues sat there quietly, staring at their cameras. “The audit team is like ‘yeah, we gotta fix this.’ And the directors were really harping on ‘this needs to be done’ and the IT team starts firing back,” Schloss explained. “It’s like ‘Why? Who’s gonna? What does it matter? No, this isn’t a high-priority find. This is maybe a medium. Yeah, it’s bad, but it’s not that bad.’” The call dragged on so long that Schloss was unable to finish presenting his findings and recommendations. The conflict was so severe that the client continued to follow up and ask him to explain what he found again for the next three years – long after he had moved on to other projects. He later learned that the auditing department controlled the bonuses for the IT team and there was a stipulation that any “high finding” would eliminate those bonuses. So they weren’t just arguing about “password” - they were really talking about the compensation for an entire division. The lesson here is more than “don’t use the word ‘password’ as a password.” It's also about misaligned incentives. Tying security posture to compensation seems like a good way to incentivize workers to follow best practices, but it also leads them to deny responsibility and minimize mistakes when they're found. ®

item.title: UK government hasn't the foggiest how much it's spending on digital transformation
item.description: The UK government says its finance systems cannot produce consistent annual figures showing how much departments and public bodies spend on digital transformation. The Science and Technology Committee's June report warned that spending was fragmented and the government lacked a clear plan for a digital state. The UK public sector spends more than £26 billion annually on digital technology, but that broad estimate does not provide a comparable departmental breakdown. Responding to the committee, the government agreed with the "intent to publish annual data on digital and data-driven spending" but said it did not "believe this is currently practicable." Existing finance systems could not "provide consistent, reliable and comparable data across departments." "The government is open to this as a direction of travel and will work with HM Treasury to consider how this could be developed over time," the response said. Committee chair Dame Chi Onwurah, who is due to address Parliament on Thirsday, said: "There's no shortage of hype about how technology can improve public services and reduce costs. Yet, frustratingly, the government cannot provide a clear picture of how much is being spent on digital transformation across departments and public bodies. "At a time when ministers are asking taxpayers to fund significant investment in technology, it's concerning that they cannot show where the money is going or how value for money is being measured. This must be addressed as a matter of urgency." The government abolished the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology in the summer, dividing its responsibilities between the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport, the Cabinet Office, and the newly created Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade. Onwurah said: "Additionally, the abolition of DSIT has only highlighted concerns about who is responsible for driving digital transformation across government. I call on the government to revisit its response and create clear leadership that can drive and deliver the scale of change needed." The committee also called for the government to end Palantir's involvement in the NHS Federated Data Platform (FDP), citing concerns over sovereignty and vendor lock-in. The relationship has drawn criticism over £60 million in earlier contracts awarded without competition. The government said it would review the FDP contract "in line with standard contract management processes to inform a decision on whether to exercise the optional two-year extension." The response did not commit to an early exit. It said any termination would have to comply with the contract's terms and public procurement law. "If a decision is taken to not extend Palantir's contract, then the contract includes controls to support transition and continuity of services, ensuring that operational delivery and patient services are protected," the response said. Onwurah said: "Additionally, the abolition of DSIT has only highlighted concerns about who is responsible for driving digital transformation across government. I call on the government to revisit its response and create clear leadership that can drive and deliver the scale of change needed." The relationship has drawn criticism over £60 million in earlier contracts awarded without competition. The government said it would review the FDP contract "in line with standard contract management processes to inform a decision on whether to exercise the optional two-year extension." The response did not commit to an early exit. It said any termination would have to comply with the contract's terms and public procurement law. "If a decision is taken to not extend Palantir's contract, then the contract includes controls to support transition and continuity of services, ensuring that operational delivery and patient services are protected," the response said. Onwurah said the committee was pleased the government had committed to developing a strategy to tackle vendor lock-in and build greater internal capacity. "Ministers should now go further by exercising the break clause in its FDP contract and take steps to reduce our dependence on a small number of large US tech firms," she added. Palantir maintains that its technology provides value for money and helps the NHS improve efficiency. ®

item.title: Nintendo Switch Sports Resort review – Wii Sports lives on in this effortlessly appealing collection of games
item.description: Nintendo Switch 2; Nintendo/Nintendo Bringing a holiday vibe and a generous selection of sport-themed games, this is exactly what you want from a family video game When the first Nintendo Switch Sports brought the effortless fun of Wii Sports back into my living room in 2022, I was frankly delighted . My small children discovered the pleasure of waving a controller around in enthusiastic imitation of a tennis player, and the surprising subtlety of virtual bowling, working out how to twist the wrist just right to guarantee a strike. I did not expect this game to become a family fixture for the next several years as my kids got older and climbed up the online ranks in all six of its sports (plus the two that were added as free updates). Switch Sports is so beloved in my household that the release of Switch Sports Resort this week is the most anticipated gaming event of the year. To be fair, my children are a bit young for Grand Theft Auto. Nintendo Switch Sports Resort brings three of the six sports back – tennis, bowling, and volleyball – alongside golf and basketball. Then there are seven entirely new sports: boxing, table tennis, archery, thumb wrestling, skateboarding, jetski, and piloting a little prop plane. They are all intuitive, easy to get the hang of on the first or second attempt – some have more legs than others, in the long run – and all of them, crucially, are a little bit silly. Thumb wrestling in particular is cheerfully absurd, giving your characters gigantic thumbs on hands the size of their heads. Continue reading...
item.dc:creator: Keza MacDonald
item.content:encoded: Nintendo Switch 2; Nintendo/Nintendo Bringing a holiday vibe and a generous selection of sport-themed games, this is exactly what you want from a family video game When the first Nintendo Switch Sports brought the effortless fun of Wii Sports back into my living room in 2022, I was frankly delighted . My small children discovered the pleasure of waving a controller around in enthusiastic imitation of a tennis player, and the surprising subtlety of virtual bowling, working out how to twist the wrist just right to guarantee a strike. I did not expect this game to become a family fixture for the next several years as my kids got older and climbed up the online ranks in all six of its sports (plus the two that were added as free updates). Switch Sports is so beloved in my household that the release of Switch Sports Resort this week is the most anticipated gaming event of the year. To be fair, my children are a bit young for Grand Theft Auto. Nintendo Switch Sports Resort brings three of the six sports back – tennis, bowling, and volleyball – alongside golf and basketball. Then there are seven entirely new sports: boxing, table tennis, archery, thumb wrestling, skateboarding, jetski, and piloting a little prop plane. They are all intuitive, easy to get the hang of on the first or second attempt – some have more legs than others, in the long run – and all of them, crucially, are a little bit silly. Thumb wrestling in particular is cheerfully absurd, giving your characters gigantic thumbs on hands the size of their heads. Continue reading...

item.title: Vendors asking forward deployed engineers to make good on trillion-dollar AI bet
item.description: During a flight on Marc Benioff’s private jet last year, the Salesforce CEO apparently subjected his company’s senior execs to a four-hour montage of Palantir CEO Alex Karp holding forth on the value of forward-deployed engineers (FDEs). The experience — which might have led anyone else to seek the emergency exit — was a lesson for Michael Spencer, Salesforce veep for finance and strategy, about the value of FDEs in boosting sales at Palantir, whose mantra is "land and expand." He shared the anecdote with the Deutsche Bank 2026 Technology Conference in August, just as the FDE boom was reaching fever pitch. For the uninitiated, vendors send FDEs to clients without tying them to a project . Effectively consultants-without-portfolio, they are expected to build something valuable, at speed, using their technology. The term is not new — Palantir claimed to have come up with it in 2007 — but the explosive growth of investment in FDEs, and their attachment to AI implementation, provokes questions about the benefits and risks involved for tech buyers. Earlier this month, AWS announced a $1 billion investment in a new Forward Deployed Engineering unit which aims to help customers build and deploy AI systems. AI poster-child Anthropic has also announced a $100 million investment in training FDEs. SAP, Salesforce and Workday — in partnership with Accenture — are heavily invested in the idea too. Salaries are on a commensurate upward trajectory. According to Levels.fyi’s Forward Deployed Engineer salary data, the US median annual total compensation was $216,250, with the 25th percentile at $180,000 and the 75th percentile at $290,000. The tech industry has an obvious problem to solve with FDEs. It spent around $1 trillion on AI last year, according to Gartner , and is set to see that figure grow by 34.7 percent in 2026. Broadly speaking, it expects to claw at least some of that money back from customers. The tech industry claims the advent of FDEs also benefits customers by helping them to access AI engineering skills, which are in short supply. Benioff told an earnings call in December last year that customers working with its FDEs were deploying Salesforce's AI technology 33 percent faster than those who were not. Nonetheless, Gartner has warned that, done badly, reliance on vendor FDEs for every change and iteration creates enormous lock-in. There is also a risk the process can leak customer intellectual property, and with it, competitive advantage. Mukul Saha, software engineering senior director at Gartner, told The Register : "The FDE engagement, generally, is that a company has an AI product and goes to the end user site, and part of the deal is they’re going to be learning things as they implement. They’re going to take back certain knowledge that makes the product better. But there's a fine line." There is a risk that those benefiting are the users' close competitors, as FDEs share information. Could an FDE be taking the user’s competitive advantage
item.dc:creator: Lindsay Clark
item.content:encoded: During a flight on Marc Benioff’s private jet last year, the Salesforce CEO apparently subjected his company’s senior execs to a four-hour montage of Palantir CEO Alex Karp holding forth on the value of forward-deployed engineers (FDEs). The experience — which might have led anyone else to seek the emergency exit — was a lesson for Michael Spencer, Salesforce veep for finance and strategy, about the value of FDEs in boosting sales at Palantir, whose mantra is "land and expand." He shared the anecdote with the Deutsche Bank 2026 Technology Conference in August, just as the FDE boom was reaching fever pitch. For the uninitiated, vendors send FDEs to clients without tying them to a project . Effectively consultants-without-portfolio, they are expected to build something valuable, at speed, using their technology. The term is not new — Palantir claimed to have come up with it in 2007 — but the explosive growth of investment in FDEs, and their attachment to AI implementation, provokes questions about the benefits and risks involved for tech buyers. Earlier this month, AWS announced a $1 billion investment in a new Forward Deployed Engineering unit which aims to help customers build and deploy AI systems. AI poster-child Anthropic has also announced a $100 million investment in training FDEs. SAP, Salesforce and Workday — in partnership with Accenture — are heavily invested in the idea too. Salaries are on a commensurate upward trajectory. According to Levels.fyi’s Forward Deployed Engineer salary data, the US median annual total compensation was $216,250, with the 25th percentile at $180,000 and the 75th percentile at $290,000. The tech industry has an obvious problem to solve with FDEs. It spent around $1 trillion on AI last year, according to Gartner , and is set to see that figure grow by 34.7 percent in 2026. Broadly speaking, it expects to claw at least some of that money back from customers. The tech industry claims the advent of FDEs also benefits customers by helping them to access AI engineering skills, which are in short supply. Benioff told an earnings call in December last year that customers working with its FDEs were deploying Salesforce's AI technology 33 percent faster than those who were not. Nonetheless, Gartner has warned that, done badly, reliance on vendor FDEs for every change and iteration creates enormous lock-in. There is also a risk the process can leak customer intellectual property, and with it, competitive advantage. Mukul Saha, software engineering senior director at Gartner, told The Register : "The FDE engagement, generally, is that a company has an AI product and goes to the end user site, and part of the deal is they’re going to be learning things as they implement. They’re going to take back certain knowledge that makes the product better. But there's a fine line." There is a risk that those benefiting are the users' close competitors, as FDEs share information. Could an FDE be taking the user’s competitive advantage and passing it on to others? Saha said: "That would be a complete violation of the IP, right? That's how fast things are moving. This is a concern I hear as I interact with end user clients." Then there is the risk of vendor lock-in. Gartner has warned that if FDEs become indispensable — because only they understand the workflows they built — keeping them full-time as consultants is neither economical nor strategic. "We're actually advising clients to understand the use cases they are going to be implementing well before FDEs come on site. If you’re doing an FDE engagement, figure out the exit strategy. Customers should figure out how they’re going to be taking over once the FDE resources go," Saha said. However, in its advisory research, Gartner said that if FDE engagements have clear guidelines on governance, business value delivery, IP ownership, project co-ownership, knowledge transfer, and an exit strategy, they can be valuable. They can get projects to production faster and increase the chances of return on investment. Where the FDE is attached to a set of products already sold to the customer by a major enterprise software vendor, there is also the difficult question of licensing and commercial arrangements. Here, users need to be careful, because these issues may not be on the FDE's radar during projects, said Craig Guarente, founder and CEO of Palisade Compliance, a software licensing advisory company. "They don't care about it. They're not even checking licensing. They're not checking tokenization. They're not checking what the customer is paying for or what the commercials are. Again, it is up to the user. It's up to the buyer of the software, of the AI tool, to make sure that what they’re doing is in line and meets their expectations," he said. Customers with open-ended contracts with the supplier could be "really exposed" if they don’t understand what FDEs are doing. Similarly, those with capped usage could find they reach their limits and have to pay for more usage, he said. Users should also be aware that it is possible FDEs could share their software usage and IT strategy with their home vendor, Guarente said, adding that he had seen no direct evidence of this practice. "Companies have a huge incentive to make sure customers turn [features] on, because if they don't, vendors can't recognize the revenue. Then, if there is a variable commercial contract, from a corporate level there are huge incentives [to get customers to use more]," he said. Similarly, there is a risk of sharing customer information within the vendor’s sales and audit departments. Guarente told us: "If you were a company and you make money from licensing your IP, why wouldn't you do that? It just makes sense. It is not just the audit department, but the sales team, customer success team and support organizations. The FDE is, like, ‘I did this for this company.’ Now they set up the next step, which could be a sales conversation or just more education. Who knows? But if I was running an AI company and I had these engineers deployed to get customers to turn on and use my stuff, that would be my first step. Let's get them hooked on it, and then ask how to generate more revenue. Obviously, one of the ways is to make the stuff better." As the tech industry strives to claw back its gargantuan AI investments, it is following Palantir’s lead and adopting the FDE strategy. Customers need to be aware of how it works and ensure they maintain control of their own AI plans. ®

item.title: Why the immediate future of liquid cooling is hybrid
item.description: From training massive language models to powering nonstop inference , AI is fundamentally rewriting the rules of data center thermal management. AI workloads are characteristically less predictable and significantly more power-dense than traditional operations. As a result, deploying liquid cooling is no longer an experimental consideration. It has become absolute table stakes for handling AI and high-performance computing (HPC) demands. The industry conversation has shifted rapidly from “if or when” to how quickly organizations can deploy and scale. Here is a look at how AI is driving the shift toward high-density thermal management , the operational realities of adopting these systems, why the near future belongs to hybrid environments, and how data center operators can successfully navigate the transition. AI Workloads Push Densities Beyond Air Alone: The Hybrid Era Historically, traditional cooling methods were sufficient for enterprise workloads. However, air cooling remains viable and efficient only up to approximately 20 to 40 kW per rack. Today’s GPU-accelerated AI racks commonly operate between 40 kW and well over 100 kW, with next-generation systems expected to push toward 200 kW or more. This GPU-driven density has made air-only cooling strategies fundamentally impractical for cutting-edge infrastructure. This extreme concentration of heat generation challenges traditional airflow-based architectures, demanding a transformation in AI data center cooling. In the ongoing evaluation of DLC vs. air (direct liquid cooling versus air cooling), t he performance data is conclusive . Thermal modeling demonstrates that single-phase direct liquid cooling maintains chip-to-coolant temperature differences of roughly 17 to 20 °C under roughly 500 W processor loads , whereas comparable air-cooled systems exceed 60 °C. Liquid cooling, which is up to 3,000 times more effective at transferring heat than air, efficiently captures heat directly at the source, preventing thermal throttling and protecting infrastructure ROI. While transitioning to liquid cooling may seem like a straightforward solution, it is rarely a sudden, wholesale replacement. Most facilities are not going all-in on liquid. Instead, they are adopting hybrid cooling models that combine traditional air architectures with advanced direct-to-chip systems. Why Hybrid Will Dominate Transitions Through 2027-2028 Through 2027 and 2028, hybrid thermal strategies will dominate because data centers must accommodate both legacy IT equipment and next-generation AI accelerators within the same facility. The reality of brownfield retrofits, where most AI capacity is initially being deployed in existing air-cooled facilities, versus designing greenfield sites for liquid from day one means that air cooling will still play a critical role in ancillary systems and lower-density zones. The future is not strictly liquid cooling only. It is about right-sizing the cooling method to the specific workload. Ope
item.dc:creator: Andrew Bradner
item.content:encoded: From training massive language models to powering nonstop inference , AI is fundamentally rewriting the rules of data center thermal management. AI workloads are characteristically less predictable and significantly more power-dense than traditional operations. As a result, deploying liquid cooling is no longer an experimental consideration. It has become absolute table stakes for handling AI and high-performance computing (HPC) demands. The industry conversation has shifted rapidly from “if or when” to how quickly organizations can deploy and scale. Here is a look at how AI is driving the shift toward high-density thermal management , the operational realities of adopting these systems, why the near future belongs to hybrid environments, and how data center operators can successfully navigate the transition. AI Workloads Push Densities Beyond Air Alone: The Hybrid Era Historically, traditional cooling methods were sufficient for enterprise workloads. However, air cooling remains viable and efficient only up to approximately 20 to 40 kW per rack. Today’s GPU-accelerated AI racks commonly operate between 40 kW and well over 100 kW, with next-generation systems expected to push toward 200 kW or more. This GPU-driven density has made air-only cooling strategies fundamentally impractical for cutting-edge infrastructure. This extreme concentration of heat generation challenges traditional airflow-based architectures, demanding a transformation in AI data center cooling. In the ongoing evaluation of DLC vs. air (direct liquid cooling versus air cooling), t he performance data is conclusive . Thermal modeling demonstrates that single-phase direct liquid cooling maintains chip-to-coolant temperature differences of roughly 17 to 20 °C under roughly 500 W processor loads , whereas comparable air-cooled systems exceed 60 °C. Liquid cooling, which is up to 3,000 times more effective at transferring heat than air, efficiently captures heat directly at the source, preventing thermal throttling and protecting infrastructure ROI. While transitioning to liquid cooling may seem like a straightforward solution, it is rarely a sudden, wholesale replacement. Most facilities are not going all-in on liquid. Instead, they are adopting hybrid cooling models that combine traditional air architectures with advanced direct-to-chip systems. Why Hybrid Will Dominate Transitions Through 2027-2028 Through 2027 and 2028, hybrid thermal strategies will dominate because data centers must accommodate both legacy IT equipment and next-generation AI accelerators within the same facility. The reality of brownfield retrofits, where most AI capacity is initially being deployed in existing air-cooled facilities, versus designing greenfield sites for liquid from day one means that air cooling will still play a critical role in ancillary systems and lower-density zones. The future is not strictly liquid cooling only. It is about right-sizing the cooling method to the specific workload. Operators will successfully scale by deploying mixed architectures, such as utilizing direct-to-chip cold plates and Coolant Distribution Units (CDUs) for dense AI clusters, while managing residual heat with Computer Room Air Handlers (CRAHs) or fan-assisted Rear-Door Heat Exchangers (RDHx). The Real Bottleneck: Operational Complexity and the Talent Gap While the technology for liquid cooling is maturing, navigating the operational complexity of a hybrid cooling environment is the real challenge. Cooling is no longer just a facilities issue. It requires the convergence of IT, mechanical engineering, and software management. Facilities must now manage fluid chemistry, leak detection, risk mitigation, and sophisticated maintenance workflows. What’s more, the industry is facing a widening talent gap. Uptime Institute reports that nearly two-thirds of operators struggle to hire and retain qualified staff, underscoring a shortage of teams with expertise across both liquid cooling systems and integrated infrastructure. Addressing this will require new training models, deeper vendor collaboration, and greater reliance on managed services. While the industry is making strides toward standardizing interoperable designs - such as plug-and-play CDUs and manifolds that distribute coolant efficiently across racks - there is still fragmentation across vendors and approaches. Additionally, operators must navigate changing economics. While liquid infrastructure requires higher upfront CapEx, it delivers better Total Cost of Ownership (TCO) over time due to enhanced efficiency and density. Decision-makers are consequently shifting their focus from what is cheapest today to what can scale with AI demand. A Blueprint for Success: Reference Architectures and Readiness Navigating this hybrid cooling transition requires standardizing deployments to avoid complex, bespoke engineering for every site. A successful liquid cooling ecosystem relies on selecting the appropriate heat rejection architectures, which are defined by the heat capture method, CDU type (rack-mounted or floor-mounted), and the method of rejecting heat outdoors. A successful blueprint involve s choosing among six core architectures, ranging from rejecting heat to air within the IT space via liquid-to-air (L-A) CDUs, to utilizing dedicated independent water systems with liquid-to-liquid (L-L) CDUs for massive deployments. To future-proof AI infrastructure, operators should utilize a strategic readiness checklist: ● Plan in Parallel: Physical infrastructure and IT planning must happen simultaneously from day one to prevent facilities from lagging behind hardware deployments. ● Design for Flexibility: Build dynamic, responsive designs capable of supporting multiple hardware generations, utilizing hybrid air and liquid combinations. ● Embrace Sustainability and Heat Reuse: Tying cooling strategies to ESG goals is a clear win, as advanced liquid cooling solutions can reduce total facility energy consumption by up to 40 percent and cut water use by 20-90 percent. Furthermore, liquid cooling unlocks opportunities for heat reuse, allowing operators to redirect waste heat to adjacent buildings or district heating systems. Derisking Adoption Through Integrated Partnerships Deploying liquid cooling at scale introduces risk, particularly when sourcing racks, power, and cooling from multiple uncoordinated vendors. To derisk adoption and bridge the talent gap, operators must lean on integrated, end-to-end partnerships. Providers like Schneider Electric are addressing this complexity by engineering fully synchronized ecosystems. Facilities can successfully derisk liquid cooling transitions by focusing on: ● Integrated Power and Cooling: At AI densities, even minor imbalances between electrical load and thermal rejection can lead to system instability, underscoring the necessity of integrated AI data center cooling solutions. Through its acquisition of Motivair, Schneider Electric now offers a complete end-to-end liquid cooling ecosystem (including CDUs, cold plates, and manifolds) that is designed to work seamlessly alongside resilient uninterruptible power supplies (UPS) and distribution units. ● Validated Designs: Collaborating early with IT vendors and chip designers helps align reference designs for optimized integration. For example, Schneider Electric’s close collaboration with NVIDIA on validated architectures helps prevent physical infrastructure from becoming a bottleneck to GPU performance. ● Digital Lifecycle Management: AI infrastructure must become more dynamic. Using digital twins and simulation software, like Schneider Electric’s ETAP and AVEVA platforms, teams can design, model, and validate integrated power and cooling architectures before physical construction begins, predicting issues before they arise. ● Global Manufacturing and Services: Sourcing from partners with robust global manufacturing capacity reduces supply chain risk and accel

item.title: Certification authority eMudhra defends its laughably weak private keys
item.description: Indian certification authority eMudhra has defended the laughably weak private keys it used to sign some digital certificates it issued, and suggested others should share the blame for the incident. In case you’re coming to this one late, news broke yesterday that private keys the company used to sign certs were beyond weak: one was literally just the number “4,” and several others were short strings of easily guessed two-or-three-digit numbers. It’s easy to deduce the value of those keys, which makes it possible to forge certs and impersonate websites or other resources. That’s gold for scammers, phishers, and other miscreants. The entire infosec industry has pointed that out, urged swift adoption of better certs, and lamented the fact that implementing replacements will be a long and thankless task. eMudhra’s statement about the incident says it generated keys during “a Key Generation Ceremony (KGC) held on April 30, 2025, using FIPS 140-2 Level 3 Hardware Security Modules (HSMs).” Such hardware is the standard kit for the job and should in theory produce nicely complex keys and store them securely. But something went wrong. “A flaw in the KGC caused a wrap/unwrap step to produce a second set of weak keys alongside the original strong keys,” the statement claims. “The weak keys were the ones published to the browser root stores. eMudhra is working to establish the root cause.” The company then gets a tad defensive. “These roots and issuing CAs have gone through independent audits for two years in a row and have been in browser trust lists since mid-2025,” the statement adds, seemingly shifting some blame to auditors and other stakeholders. The announcement then points out that eMudhra’s TLS business generates just one percent of its revenue, meaning this mess won’t impact its bottom line too much. That’s nice to know for the company’s investors but rather misses the point that whoever relies on the company now has an urgent, unwanted, and costly job to do replacing certs. “eMudhra is working directly with customers who may be affected to give them replacement certificates, so that critical services are not disrupted. The company is also working with the root programs and continues its root-cause investigation,” the statement adds. The company allows that the incident “may have some reputational risks on eMudhra which cannot be quantified.” Ya think? ®

item.title: AI firms say UK has a year to head off datacentre protests before construction is threatened
item.description: Exclusive: Nvidia, Microsoft and Cisco taskforce urges ministers to offer areas greater benefits from tech infrastructure amid fears of US-style opposition AI companies have told ministers they have 12 months to head off public opposition to datacentres in the UK or risk US-style protests that could threaten their construction. Successive dry summers and rising energy bills are increasing public scrutiny of plans for the huge computer warehouses that are used to train and run AI models, says a submission to the Labour government from a group including the AI infrastructure companies Nvidia, Microsoft and Cisco. Continue reading...

item.title: IBM CEO says open weight models are now irresistibly good and cheap on-prem
item.description: IBM CEO Arvind Krishna has told investors that open weight models now make brilliant sense for on-prem enterprise use. Speaking on the company’s Q3 earnings call, Krishna said that in 2024 closed frontier models were plainly superior to open alternatives. “If you ran some assessment, some benchmark, and it was broad-based, not narrow, the top model might score a 70, and the open model might score a 20 or a 30.” “In late 2025, we began to see that gap shrink, where maybe the gap was not 70 to 20 or 30, it was 70 to 50,” he continued. The CEO said open weight models currently deliver “anywhere from 25 percent to 10 percent of the token cost of the frontier models. That is very attractive given that they’re now 90 percent as effective.” “It’s a simple question for any enterprise. Would you like something that’s 10 percent of the cost if it’s 90 percent as good as the best, or do you want to pay that 10 times higher cost?” Krishna thinks businesses will most often choose not to incur the higher costs. “Then the question is: how many tasks require that? I would tell you some do, but the vast majority, summarizing an email, examining a contract, answering a customer call, composing an email, all of those can be done as well with the much cheaper answer.” The CEO said those numbers mean IBM is seeing booming interest in on-prem AI infrastructure. While he thinks most businesses can build useful AI infrastructure in just two or three racks, he feels many will struggle to get it running. “The question becomes: how do you do that?” he said. “The question that the enterprise struggles with is: ‘Where are my kernel engineers? Where are the people who worry about the underlying network? Who can make sure that the model is clustered on GPUs that are close to each other in network proximity? Who can make sure that you’re doing the right caching of results so you get an incredible response?’” He didn’t have answers, other than to say IBM will produce software that eases AI deployments. Krishna also predicted demand for on-prem AI will spur sales of Big Blue’s Spyre mainframe accelerator cards. The CEO said current-gen z17 mainframes have delivered $1bn more revenue than any previous model, and said Big Blue’s new rackable models delivered “the strongest midrange launch in IBM Z in nearly two decades.” Mainframe revenue, however, fell 20 percent – as IBM expects given it’s now 18 months since it launched the z17. IBM’s infrastructure revenue grew five percent year-over-year to $3.7 billion, much slower improvement than recorded by rivals Dell, HPE, and Lenovo. Some of that future revenue is for Red Hat’s virtualization products, which have now won $800 million of deals, with a pipeline of a further $750 million. Some of that future revenue is for Red Hat’s virtualization products, which have now won $800 million of deals, with a pipeline of a further $750 million. That’s a solid result for a product line launched in 2024, and IBM believes there’s more to come given the possibility some VMware users are on the move. Total quarterly revenue hit $17.1 billion, up five percent. IBM’s share price wobbled in after-hours trading and ended down a point or two. ‘Emergency maintenance’ for IBM Cloud Another IBM matter The Register is watching today is a severity one incident in the Big Blue cloud, caused by “emergency maintenance” that meant users could not provision new resources or virtual private clouds for 90 minutes. Users of IBM’s Classic Cloud, the service it acquired from SoftLayer in 2013, have been told Big Blue will “restore new provisioning and resource management in our Classic environment” by 08:00 UTC on Thursday – meaning the incident will last at least 16 hours. IBM commenced that work a handful of hours after the announcement of critical bugs in PHP . We’ve asked if fixing that flaw is the reason for the incident and will update this story if we get a response. ®

item.title: Philippine government suspends top tech official for alleged misconduct
item.description: The Philippines government’s Ombudsman has suspended a senior Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT) official over allegations he assigned government contracts to a company he founded and continued to hold a stake in. The Ombudsman announced the suspension yesterday and named Undersecretary for E-Government David L. Almirol as the individual of concern, after considering “administrative complaints of Grave Misconduct, Conduct Prejudicial to the Best Interest of the Service and violation of … the Code of Conduct and Ethical Standards for Public Officials and Employees.” “In ordering the preventive suspension, the Ombudsman found strong evidence supporting the administrative charges against Almirol,” according to its announcement of the suspension. Almirol founded a company called Multisys Technologies Corporation that offers software development services, plus packaged products. After over a decade as the company’s CEO, Almirol in 2022 joined DICT at the request of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., to work on improving e-government services. The Ombudsman alleged that between 2023 and 2025 DICT awarded at least eight contracts valued at over ₱1.5 billion ($24 million) to entities linked with Multisys. The contracts covered information and communications technology consultancy, e-government application deployment, web-based messaging services, cloud infrastructure, data center colocation and software subscriptions. Evidence of those transactions is apparently on the record in Multisys’s books. Local laws mean Almirol should have divested his stake in Multisys within 60 days. The Ombudsman alleges the exec missed that deadline but later complied. It’s not alleged he issued contracts in the period during which he continued to hold Multisys shares. The Ombudsman has suspended Almirol without pay for six months, a step it says is necessary because if he continued in the role it “could prejudice the investigation, particularly given his control and custody of documents and evidence relevant to the case.” The org has also pointed out that its decision does not pre-judge the matter, but is “a precautionary measure intended to preserve the integrity of the proceedings and ensure an impartial and unimpeded investigation.” President Marcos Jr. made rooting out corruption a key plank of his platform and even created an agency to tackle the problem. However, it’s felt that some anti-corruption actions may have been partly politically motivated. Past tech-related scandals in the Philippines include a 2022 case that saw its Department of Education overpay for lousy laptops . ®

item.title: Canadian publisher Boréal ends relationship with novelist Thélyson Orélien over alleged use of AI
item.description: Author withdrawn from France’s Prix Goncourt last month has repeatedly denied using artificial intelligence to write novel The publisher of top-selling Haitian Canadian writer Thélyson Orélien, who was removed from France’s most prestigious literary prize list last month, has confirmed the author used artificial intelligence to help write his novel C’était ça ou mourir (It Was Either That or Die). Orélien has denied allegations that he used AI on his breakthrough novel and, last week, Canadian publisher Les Éditions du Boréal said it was standing by the 38-year-old writer. Continue reading...

item.title: To help world gorge on GPUs, Nvidia brings cash bucket to fatten wafer-thin supply chain
item.description: Nvidia has decided that its future prospects rest on an improved silicon substrate and packing supply chain, so has dipped into its giant pile of cash to ensure it can get the parts it needs by ensuring its suppliers have the resources needed to play their small part in keeping the flow of GPUs and AI processors strong. It’s not unusual for manufacturers to invest in their suppliers, because it helps to create certainty and spread financial risk. For those deals to be announced at a major tech company’s conference – as Nvidia did at its Berlin GTC gabfest – is somewhat novel, suggesting the company feels the need to show investors it is working to ensure it can meet demand for its products, and that demand will persist for years. Several of Nvidia’s announcements pertained to silicon substrates, aka wafers. Whatever you call them, they’re blank, round, silicon slabs onto which chipmakers etch circuits. They’re made by companies that sell to foundries like TSMC and Intel, which then turn them into chips of various flavours. At GTC Berlin, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang observed that demand for AI hardware is vast, but that “Capacity is the constraint.” Specifically, capacity for activities like building substrates, advanced silicon packaging, testing, and creating optical connectors. Big Green therefore plans to increase substrate capacity for its products by 2.5x over the next three years. To make that happen, Nvidia has added Samsung’s Electro-Mechanics business unit to its substrate supply chain. Samsung apparently has immediate capacity at a factory in South Korea and Nvidia intends to tap that now. The deal means that by 2028, about a quarter of Sammy’s substrate output will go to Nvidia. Nvidia already has a deal with Japanese substrate outfit IBIDEN. In Berlin, the GPU giant pointed to further expansion that will triple production at an IBIDEN plant. Taiwanese substrate player Unimicron is also benefiting from Nvidia’s generosity, in the form of a capacity reservation agreement and associated plant expansion plans. It’s not just wafers that Nvidia wants to tuck into. The company has also signed a capacity reservation with Korean silicon packaging player Amkor. Again, Big Green’s involvement will see its partner expand capacity, in this case by 300 percent. Nvidia says this deal “will support higher production volumes for current and next-generation platforms.” AI systems need speedy networks, and many players see optical connections as the best way to build systems capable of handling the data deluges modern workloads create and require. Nvidia has therefore hatched a plan to boost manufacturing capacity at optics outfit SPIL. Again, Big Green already has a deal with the company, but in Berlin it expanded that arrangement in the hope it expands production capacity 15x by mid-2027, then doubles that again by the end of 2028. All of which suggests that Nvidia believes the AI infrastructure boom has years left to run. ®

item.title: Meta ordered to pay $25bn to New Mexico in Cambridge Analytica data-privacy case
item.description: Jury had found Meta misled consumers after Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign obtained user data without consent A judge in New Mexico ordered Meta Platforms to pay $25bn on ⁠Wednesday after a jury found the company had misled consumers in a case arising from allegations that a political consulting firm involved in Donald Trump ’s 2016 presidential campaign obtained data from millions of Facebook users ⁠without their consent. “Facebook’s wrongdoing – ⁠over the course of ​years and systematically broadcast to the public – goes to the heart of Facebook’s core business practices,” Judge Francis Mathew wrote in his order after the verdict. Continue reading...

item.title: Tesla beats earnings projections after Musk floats SpaceX merger plan
item.description: Musk says ‘there’s a lot of merit’ to potential merger that would require approval of 50% of all Tesla shareholders, but declined to elaborate Investors were paying close attention to Tesla ’s third-quarter earnings call on Wednesday afternoon, after chief executive Elon Musk floated the idea of merging the car company with his rocket and AI company, SpaceX . But they didn’t glean further information after the company announced there would be no questions on the matter. “With regard to a potential merger with SpaceX, I think I said everything that should be said yesterday,” Musk, the CEO of both companies, said on Tesla’s earnings call. He repeated a phrase he said on Tuesday: “I feel like I’m tap dancing through a minefield.” Continue reading...

item.title: PHP blames supply chain security biz Chainguard for putting huge chunks of the web at risk
item.description: PHP developers have accused software supply chain security shop Chainguard of effectively revealing critical bugs in the open-source scripting language ahead of a planned official disclosure. On Wednesday, just hours after releasing emergency patches for the two bugs collectively called PHP2shell, PHP maintainers published a blog about how the vulnerabilities were found and fixed. They credited researchers at Calif, OpenAI, and Wiz with finding the security holes between August and September. All three companies have said they used AI models to find the vulnerabilities, which are now tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, and can allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute code on servers running PHP. This is especially serious because PHP powers huge chunks of the public web. It also adds a dose of irony to the “leak and disrupted disclosure” part of the blog, which blames Chainguard - a company that aims to secure software supply chains by hardening open source code - for the messy disclosure. The trouble, according to PHP developers, started on Tuesday around 15:00 UTC, when “two CVE IDs began circulating on online forums and social media,” along with incorrect information about the release time and CVSS severity rating. At that point, no technical details leaked. The rumors, however, prompted PHP maintainers to warn people in advance about the critical flaws, and move the planned disclosure forward a day, from Thursday to Wednesday. “Distributors were still packaging the fix, so releasing immediately would have left many users without an easy way to update,” the PHP Foundation blog says. “Moving the release forward by one day was the best compromise between acting quickly, giving people time to prepare, and making sure everyone had a simple update path when the vulnerabilities were disclosed.” A couple of hours later, Calif “mistakenly” published a video showing a proof-of-concept exploit and “additional, though limited” information about the bugs, we’re told. “Mitigation advice we started providing to a few critical infrastructure providers around Oct 20th 23:00 UTC, may have leaked as well,” the PHP blog says, but it does not name these providers. And then it throws Chainguard under the bus: “On October 21st at 07:41 UTC, more than six hours before the coordinated release, Chainguard unilaterally broke the embargo and published built images containing the fix. Like other distributors, Chainguard had received the patch in advance so its users could update the moment the vulnerabilities were disclosed. Any attacker could now study the fix in binary form while every other PHP user was still waiting for the release. This disregarded weeks of work by many parties toward a coordinated disclosure.” Chainguard CEO: 'We made the call' Chainguard CEO Dan Lorenc spoke with The Register on Wednesday, and while he doesn’t dispute the timeline, said his company "didn't leak." “These things are messy,” Lorenc said. Chainguard learned “something
item.dc:creator: Jessica Lyons
item.content:encoded: PHP developers have accused software supply chain security shop Chainguard of effectively revealing critical bugs in the open-source scripting language ahead of a planned official disclosure. On Wednesday, just hours after releasing emergency patches for the two bugs collectively called PHP2shell, PHP maintainers published a blog about how the vulnerabilities were found and fixed. They credited researchers at Calif, OpenAI, and Wiz with finding the security holes between August and September. All three companies have said they used AI models to find the vulnerabilities, which are now tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, and can allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute code on servers running PHP. This is especially serious because PHP powers huge chunks of the public web. It also adds a dose of irony to the “leak and disrupted disclosure” part of the blog, which blames Chainguard - a company that aims to secure software supply chains by hardening open source code - for the messy disclosure. The trouble, according to PHP developers, started on Tuesday around 15:00 UTC, when “two CVE IDs began circulating on online forums and social media,” along with incorrect information about the release time and CVSS severity rating. At that point, no technical details leaked. The rumors, however, prompted PHP maintainers to warn people in advance about the critical flaws, and move the planned disclosure forward a day, from Thursday to Wednesday. “Distributors were still packaging the fix, so releasing immediately would have left many users without an easy way to update,” the PHP Foundation blog says. “Moving the release forward by one day was the best compromise between acting quickly, giving people time to prepare, and making sure everyone had a simple update path when the vulnerabilities were disclosed.” A couple of hours later, Calif “mistakenly” published a video showing a proof-of-concept exploit and “additional, though limited” information about the bugs, we’re told. “Mitigation advice we started providing to a few critical infrastructure providers around Oct 20th 23:00 UTC, may have leaked as well,” the PHP blog says, but it does not name these providers. And then it throws Chainguard under the bus: “On October 21st at 07:41 UTC, more than six hours before the coordinated release, Chainguard unilaterally broke the embargo and published built images containing the fix. Like other distributors, Chainguard had received the patch in advance so its users could update the moment the vulnerabilities were disclosed. Any attacker could now study the fix in binary form while every other PHP user was still waiting for the release. This disregarded weeks of work by many parties toward a coordinated disclosure.” Chainguard CEO: 'We made the call' Chainguard CEO Dan Lorenc spoke with The Register on Wednesday, and while he doesn’t dispute the timeline, said his company "didn't leak." “These things are messy,” Lorenc said. Chainguard learned “something was coming in PHP” on Friday from one of the researchers that found the bugs, Lorenc told us. Later that night, using his company’s AI harness and a frontier model, the CEO and the Chainguard team independently found the same memory corruption vulnerabilities. All it took was a “basic prompt of ‘find bad vulnerabilities in PHP,’” Lorenc wrote in a subsequent LinkedIn post. On Saturday, Chainguard began working with the PHP maintainers, confirmed that some of its findings matched the bug reports, and helped test the patches. “The patches are crazy - this is not a simple vulnerability,” Lorenc told The Register . “It really did take them months to build a real, working patch for it. And then on Monday, the rumors started, and yesterday it just spiraled.” Some people published POCs on social media, other security vendors reported seeing real-world exploitation, and late Tuesday night Lorenc told us he decided to ship the fixes, and notified the PHP coordinated disclosure channel about his plans. “People were getting hit in advance” of the official PHP disclosure, “so we made the call to ship the fixes under that,” Lorenc said. “It's coordinated vulnerability disclosure, unless there's evidence of active exploits in the wild.” Also on Tuesday night, Chainguard published built artifacts and made them accessible to anyone, not just customers. “And then I woke up this morning and saw that this was all our fault,” Lorenc said. When asked if he would do anything differently, given the fallout from Chainguard’s early disclosure, Lorenc said no. “This process and policy is based on trying to coordinate as much as possible until shit hits the fan and people start weaponizing things,” he said. “It sucks, because we really are all on one team, and there's bad guys over there doing stuff.” Chainguard’s honeypots trapped IPs from China and Russia targeting the vulnerabilities on Wednesday, Lorenc added. “Just being told there's a vulnerability in a piece of software - even something as big as PHP - is enough to find it,” he told us. “I did that myself without any other knowledge on Friday." "I think this is kind of the new normal. People are able to build an exploit in hours without even knowing what the vulnerability is." What we know about the CVEs and how to exploit them While we still don’t know the scope of exploitation - or what will happen to vulnerable legacy systems that don’t have security fixes - threat hunters predict it’s going to be a doozy. “Successful exploitation could allow attackers to take control of affected servers, steal sensitive data, and deface the websites running on them,” Wiz researchers Sagi Tzadik, Shir Tamari, Nir Ohfeld, and Tomer Schwartz warned on Wednesday, adding the oft-quoted stat that PHP powers 70 percent of all websites in the world. “Every PHP version released in the last decade is affected by at least one of these vulnerabilities, going back to version 5.4,” the Wiz kids wrote. “Attackers can exploit them remotely, in some cases fairly easily. Immediate patching is strongly advised.” Both bugs are related to how PHP handles memory management and error handling, and both lead to remote code execution (RCE). They can cause a corrupted internal PHP state when a request ends unexpectedly, and then a later request can reuse that state, leading to memory disclosure or RCE. “Both are memory corruption vulnerabilities,” VulnCheck researcher Patrick Garrity explained. “If an attacker can shape the memory PHP trusts, they can potentially hijack what it does next, and in these cases that means remote code execution.” CVE-2026-109618 ( GHSA-w8hw-w9fx-j79w ) leads to RCE via out-of-memory corruption. “If a request reached PHP's memory_limit at exactly the wrong moment, PHP could leave partially initialized internal data behind and later treat it as valid, corrupting memory,” the project maintainer wrote. “On Apache with mod_php, an unauthenticated request can trigger this before any application code runs.” CVE-2026-109619 ( GHSA-6wmf-4rv5-p3rp ) allows RCE via stale state. “A fatal error at the wrong point could leave internal state pointing to memory that belonged to a previous request,” according to the PGP Foundation. “A later request handled by the same worker could then use that freed memory. A use-after-free and worker crash were confirmed, and the reporter demonstrated remote code execution against a real-world application running on Apache with mod_php.”®

item.title: FCC chair warns media not to run the "fake polls" Trump keeps complaining about
item.description: Federal Communications Commission Chairman Brendan Carr today warned broadcasters about airing "fake polls," amplifying one of the many complaints that President Trump has regularly made about the news media. Carr's post on X said, "Many journalists and broadcasters have been amplifying or airing these Polls without regard to basic journalistic ethics and without informing the public that those Polls lack a scientific, accurate, or even real basis... Broadcasters are advised to avoid engaging in News Distortions or running Broadcast Hoaxes by airing Polls that would violate their regulatory obligations." Carr urged broadcasters to "provide their viewers with additional context and information about Polls they have covered." In fact, one small polling outfit was exposed as a hoax this week, and a similar incident occurred in August. News outlets have reported on these hoaxes, providing the very "context" that Carr said is needed. Read full article Comments

item.title: Xbox wants you to pay 24 to 40 cents per hour to stream games you already bought
item.description: In September, when Microsoft severely limited the game-streaming buffet available to Game Pass subscribers , the company said non-subscribers would soon be able to "purchase cloud playtime hours through the Xbox Store and stream eligible games they own on supported devices." Today, Microsoft rolled out those a la carte Cloud Playtime purchases to Xbox Insiders, with prices that might be a bit galling for players who have already purchased these streamable games. The "introductory launch pricing" for Xbox's Cloud Playtime purchases is as follows: 10 hours for $4 (~$0.40/hour) 25 hours for $8 (~$0.32/hour) 50 hours for $12 (~$0.24/hour) Purchased playtime "remains available until it’s used," Microsoft writes, so you don't have to worry about your 50-hour purchase expiring before you can use it fully. Read full article Comments
