item.title: The spec is the new code, so brush up on your prose, says Kaseya CTO
item.description: Software developers will need to get their kicks from becoming code coaches of AI, professors of prompt engineering, and masters of their domain. So says Pratik Wadher, chief technology officer at Kaseya, who oversaw a team of codesmiths rewriting software across the company’s managed services portfolio, which spans remote monitoring and management, backup and recovery, cybersecurity, and automation. “The goal is unifying our data, unifying our API, but as we are starting to also look at the product portfolio that we have, we're trying to understand what are the patterns that we can use to consolidate the product workflows,” he tells The Register . Storage is a good example. The basic workflows involve reading and writing data to storage arrays, Kaseya's own cloud environment, or the racks run by hyperscalers. The team re-architected the back end of its storage products so the storage engine reads and writes to any kind of storage from ZFS to S3. “This is where AI helps,” Wadher claims. “Fundamentally we have accelerated that piece of re-architecture.” Since joining Kaseya in September 2025, the CTO has been trying to simplify what he admits can be a “confusing” number of individual products. “The storage layer that we've been writing, we re-architected and wrote it in six weeks. And that's the actual writing, implementing and testing the code. There are years of domain expertise behind understanding how we want to write it.” In the process, Kaseya used Anthropic coding agents to help a human write the spec. The meatbags at Kaseya then iterated on it and peer-reviewed it with critique agents, before the AI generated the code. Anthropic’s Claude is becoming the “de facto standard” for writing code at Kaseya . “ When I look at my engineers, it's not how I used to write code. It's almost like I'm manipulating these agents, but the best engineers are still critical, because you have developed a lot of experience in understanding what you need to do,” Wadher says. Does this take the fun out of coding? Yes and no, he claims. Mirroring the wider industry, some Kaseya engineers are embracing the new approach and some are more “hesitant.” “ The fun part of coding is going to be the design, the architecture, the thinking. Writing code is fun but I don't think it's [ the ] fun [part]. The fun part is having the code run, seeing what it can do, and then tweaking it and changing it. If you can accelerate that and start seeing the results, I think that, for me at least, that would be the fun part: seeing the impact.” Developers must become proficient prompters and “you need the domain expertise,” he adds. “If you’re just using AI to generate code I don’t think you’re going to be useful and I don't think the code you're writing is going to be useful.” Some Reg readers and some of the article-writing vultures may disagree. It's almost like I'm manipulating these agents, but the best engineers are still critical, because you have developed a lot of experience in understanding what you need to do,” Wadher says. Does this take the fun out of coding? Yes and no, he claims. Mirroring the wider industry, some Kaseya engineers are embracing the new approach and some are more “hesitant.” “ The fun part of coding is going to be the design, the architecture, the thinking. Writing code is fun but I don't think it's [ the ] fun [part]. The fun part is having the code run, seeing what it can do, and then tweaking it and changing it. If you can accelerate that and start seeing the results, I think that, for me at least, that would be the fun part: seeing the impact.” Developers must become proficient prompters and “you need the domain expertise,” he adds. “If you’re just using AI to generate code I don’t think you’re going to be useful and I don't think the code you're writing is going to be useful.” Some Reg readers and some of the article-writing vultures may disagree. There is a clear split happening in the world of FOSS, for example, where some projects want only human-written code and others take what they describe as a more pragmatic view of AI tools . AI is already forcing change upon the tech sector. Research last year suggested the number of graduates starting a career in technology is plunging with certain functions being subsumed by agents. “I think basic tasks will be done by AI, so you're not going to need that,” Wadher says. “The skills that will be extremely important are critical thinking and writing. “The worst part of coding, [the thing] engineers hate is writing the documentation. Well, guess what? That is going to become even more critical now. Being able to write clear, concise design specifications, the functional specifications, is going to be extremely important. The good thing is that you’ll now have an [AI] partner that can do this with you and you can iterate with this partner. “I would say the new code is the spec. That's what you're going to check into GitHub now, because you want to make sure that the spec you wrote is going to generate the same type of code now over and over again. I have seen variances." ®

item.title: Happiness is the next AI KPI if Oxford boffins have their way
item.description: Mass unemployment, boiling the planet, and human extinction within a decade: the dystopian visions of AI are well rehearsed. Academics now argue that EU policymakers should ensure the taxpayers helping to fund the tech get something back, a “happiness dividend.” Researchers at the Oxford Internet Institute (OII), led by Professor Sandra Wachter, say citizens who are inadvertently helping to create the next generation of tech billionaires need more than promises that AI will boost economic growth and fatten corporate profits. Their paper, " Optimising for happiness in EU technology policy to repay public subsidies for AI ," published in the Royal Society Open Science, notes that the public backs AI development through funding, tax breaks, and access to land, water, energy, infrastructure, and data. On data, most people have no say in the matter. Creative work, social media posts, and user interactions have all been swept up to train frontier models, spurring a stream of lawsuits . The OII team proposes happiness as a third goal for AI heavyweights, alongside economic growth and risk mitigation. “Making technology less harmful is not the same as making it socially beneficial,” the researchers told us. What makes people happy? The researchers point to relatedness, competence, and autonomy, all of which some uses of AI could undermine. Chatbots that mimic human emotion may erode the value people place on real human connection. Heavy reliance on AI could dull skills . AI influence could make it harder for people to make their own choices . And datacenters threaten land and water, leaving fewer trees and green spaces for people to connect with nature. “Under the proposed approach, companies benefiting from public support would be expected to predict how their technologies will improve happiness and well-being, and be held accountable for delivering those benefits,” the researchers said. The EU has allocated €20 billion for AI gigafactories , while GenAI4EU and the Digital Europe programme is using €700 million through Horizon research projects into generative AI and supercomputing initiatives. “The public already pays for AI through subsidies, resources, and data, yet has little say over what it gets in return,” said lead author Professor Sandra Wachter. “We believe people deserve technology that increases their happiness. If the public is helping to build the AI industry, it should also share in its benefits.” Denser, more powerful servers in a growing number of datacenters are drawing more energy, potentially pushing up household electricity bills . Memory makers are prioritizing higher-margin chips, so ordinary DRAM and NAND cost more, and so do the devices that use them . Water, which some see as the planet’s next most precious commodity, is being used to cool server racks . Water, which some see as the planet’s next most precious commodity, is being used to cool server racks . Anthropic warned this year that humanity risks courting extinction unless powerful models are properly controlled. Last year it and OpenAI raised the prospect of mass unemployment as employers turn to AI to cut costs. The researchers add that the difficulty of getting data out of model makers and their cloud providers makes it harder to gauge the environmental damage datacenters are doing. Against that backdrop, finding some way to improve people’s well-being looks essential. Will the model makers take note? Even pessimists are sometimes pleasantly surprised, though we expect profits will trump pleasantness. ®

item.title: MPs urge UK government to play venture capitalist with taxpayer-funded tech
item.description: Britain is funding the next generation of tech companies without making sure taxpayers get a slice of the action, MPs have warned. In a new report shared with The Register ahead of publication, the Public Accounts Committee (PAC) has accused UK Research and Innovation (UKRI) of being overly cautious about protecting taxpayers' interests. Rather than simply handing out grants, MPs want UKRI to consider taking equity stakes in more of the businesses it backs, giving the public a chance to cash in when those companies succeed. According to the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology (DSIT), UK universities produce more spinouts and patents per pound of research funding than their US counterparts. But Britain is less adept at cashing in on its inventions. British startups still struggle to attract the investment needed to grow without moving overseas, while universities have a patchy record when it comes to exploiting their intellectual property. UKRI, meanwhile, has been reluctant to impose tougher conditions on the research it funds, arguing that doing so could discourage companies from growing. “This approach is far too cautious and we urge the Department to do much more to recover taxpayer's money when a successful company exploits research which the taxpayer, via UKRI, has paid for," the PAC said. It wants UKRI to review its standard funding terms, including whether it should take equity stakes in more companies benefiting from public money. Sir Geoffrey Clifton-Brown, chair of the PAC, acknowledged that calling for the government to behave more like a venture capitalist might seem an odd position for a committee normally concerned with keeping public spending in check. "It may strike followers of this Committee's work that our call for government to take a less cautious approach to taking a direct stake in British innovation is an unusual one," he said. "But we are a body dedicated to value for taxpayers' money, not hoarding it. The nations currently leading the global tech race did not achieve their positions by avoiding more entrepreneurial policies. This is a simple case for the government of nothing ventured, nothing gained." The government has made some effort to help British tech firms. UKRI gives AI startups free access to taxpayer-funded supercomputers, while DSIT has changed its procurement rules to give UK companies a better shot at supplying £400 million worth of specialist AI chips. The British Business Bank is also investing alongside pension funds, giving taxpayers a stake in some of the businesses receiving support. But efforts to attract more pension fund investment have been slower than ministers hoped, and MPs want DSIT to start measuring whether its various support schemes are actually helping British companies grow, rather than simply counting how much money it hands out. British startups still struggle to attract the investment needed to grow without moving overseas, while universities have a patchy record when it comes to exploiting their intellectual property. UKRI, meanwhile, has been reluctant to impose tougher conditions on the research it funds, arguing that doing so could discourage companies from growing. “This approach is far too cautious and we urge the Department to do much more to recover taxpayer's money when a successful company exploits research which the taxpayer, via UKRI, has paid for," the PAC said. It wants UKRI to review its standard funding terms, including whether it should take equity stakes in more companies benefiting from public money. Sir Geoffrey Clifton-Brown, chair of the PAC, acknowledged that calling for the government to behave more like a venture capitalist might seem an odd position for a committee normally concerned with keeping public spending in check. "It may strike followers of this Committee's work that our call for government to take a less cautious approach to taking a direct stake in British innovation is an unusual one," he said. "But we are a body dedicated to value for taxpayers' money, not hoarding it. The nations currently leading the global tech race did not achieve their positions by avoiding more entrepreneurial policies. This is a simple case for the government of nothing ventured, nothing gained." The government has made some effort to help British tech firms. UKRI gives AI startups free access to taxpayer-funded supercomputers, while DSIT has changed its procurement rules to give UK companies a better shot at supplying £400 million worth of specialist AI chips. The British Business Bank is also investing alongside pension funds, giving taxpayers a stake in some of the businesses receiving support. But efforts to attract more pension fund investment have been slower than ministers hoped, and MPs want DSIT to start measuring whether its various support schemes are actually helping British companies grow, rather than simply counting how much money it hands out. There's also the question of where all that research funding ends up. London, the South East, and the East of England continue to receive half of UKRI's funding, despite years of government promises to spread investment more evenly across the country. The North's share has improved from 12 to 20 percent over the past five years, but UKRI has yet to set specific regional funding targets. Clifton-Brown described the divide as "continuing and unacceptable," warning that progress could easily be reversed without a more deliberate effort to spread the cash around. And while MPs want UKRI to be more adventurous with its investments, they're considerably less impressed with how it manages some of the projects already on its books. The committee pointed to an airborne laboratory upgrade that UKRI abandoned after spending £46 million of its £49 million budget. Funding was finally canceled five years after the decision to upgrade the aircraft, prompting MPs to question why the plug hadn't been pulled sooner. Elsewhere, around 45 percent of the Science and Technology Facilities Council's estate is in unacceptable condition, and restoring university-owned research infrastructure to full working order would cost an estimated £5.6 billion. The PAC also criticized UKRI for failing to ensure a replacement for the ARCHER2 national supercomputer would be ready before the existing machine shuts down, leaving an expected 13-month gap. It seems Whitehall has mastered the art of spending money on innovation, but getting any back is another matter. ®

item.title: UK watchdogs urged to tackle suicide social media content after death of girl, 14
item.description: Adriana Retyte took her own life after viewing ‘high-risk’ material on the video-sharing platform TikTok A 14-year-old schoolgirl’s death after TikTok served her suicide content has prompted renewed calls for UK watchdogs to crack down on “toxic” social media feeds. Adriana Retyte, a pupil at Langley school in Norfolk, took her own life after she viewed videos and images related to suicide on the video-sharing platform, according to a coroner who last week found her access to the material on TikTok “may have played a significant part in her decision to take her life”. Continue reading...

item.title: Nervous ISPs replace Chrome as strange consumers of DNS resources
item.description: Google has fixed the flaws in the Chromium browser engine that saw it poll DNS root servers, but ISPs who seem to have odd views about resilience now emerged as a new source of probably-well-meaning overconsumption of internet resources. ICANN’s office of the Chief Technology Officer delivered that view on Monday during the governance org’s annual conference in Bali, Indonesia, in a session that shared recent data from its Identifier Technology Health Indicators (ITHI) research program which monitors the security, stability and resilience of the domain name system. ICANN principal technologist Maud Durand opened with a discussion of “Chromioids” the odd flaw in Chrome that meant well-meaning efforts to avoid a form of DNS hijacking caused the browser to generate about half of all DNS root server traffic during the year 2020. Given Chrome’s enormous prevalence, that traffic was unwelcome. ICANN, plus other internetworking and governance stakeholders, told Google to sort it out. Durand said the Chocolate Factory gradually did. ICANN has kept measuring the impact Chrome makes and Durand shared the graph below which shows the browser’s share of DNS root server traffic falling from 45 percent to one percent today. Or as Durand described it, “in the noise.” ICANN has now detected a new source of odd DNS traffic: ISPs that use multiple DNS servers for every one of their customers’ requests. “Every single DNS query is sent three times: to Google, to Cloudflare, and to another DNS resolver,” Durand said, labelling this practice a “belt and suspenders” approach because a single resolver usually suffices to keep services up. It’s good practice to specify primary and secondary DNS resolvers, in case one doesn’t work. But DNS resolvers are already very resilient, and making multiple requests is unusual. The ISPs ICANN has spotted send DNS requests over IPv4 and IPv6, and for non-cached requests repeat them within 100 milliseconds for about half of queries. A further 30 percent repeat within thirty seconds. “It is hard to know if it is a bug or a specific behaviour,” Durand said, before advancing a personal theory that the ISPs who use this odd resilience technique can’t hire skilled internetworking engineers and therefore created a kind of brute-force resilience routine. The organization is researching the cause. ICANN feels the ISPs using this practice aren’t major players, but the org worries that if the practice becomes widespread, or is adopted by a large entity, it could have a nasty impact. Pointlessly busy DNS servers also matter because ICANN thinks the number of DNS service providers is becoming more concentrated. ICANN has tried to calculate how many DNS resolvers half of internet users can “see” when they are online. As the graph below shows, users could see almost 250 resolver farms in the year 2020. item.title: Indian certification authority eMudhra’s private keys compromised – one of them was the number ‘4’
item.description: Tragically simple private keys used by a certification authority based in India have been compromised, meaning the 60-million-plus certs it has issued can’t be trusted and necessitating a massive clean-up job. The CA of concern in this case is called eMudhra, which boasts of having issued over 60 million digital certificates to help usher in a world of digital trust. The company has instead panicked the world. News of the company’s errors appeared on Tuesday in a post by Dennis Jackson, a member of Mozilla’s cryptography engineering team. “On Saturday, October 17, at 20:06 UTC, Mozilla received a report from a community member that private keys associated with eight eMudhra intermediate certificates had been compromised,” he wrote . “These keys could allow attackers to issue fraudulent HTTPS certificates for websites they do not control.” Or as Cloudflare put it , “an attacker can create a forged certificate for any domain and use it to impersonate servers to intercept or modify traffic.” Jackson has since elaborated on the incident and the response, which has thankfully seen Mozilla, Chrome, and Apple remediate the issue so their browsers won’t rely on the certificates – at least after users install an update. He also reports that eMudhra has revoked the certs, and lists many FOSS projects that have issued updates that mean they won’t recognize certs from eMudhra. That’s welcome, but sadly certs signed with these private keys are still out there and many services rely on them. Browser makers are set up to detect and reject bad certs. Others who relied on them may not be, and will likely need to dig into their environments to see if they rely on certs signed by eMudhra. Developer Geoffrey Huntley has offered some advice on automating that process. At the time of writing, eMudhra has not responded to The Register ’s inquiries about the incident and its security practices. The latter question is of great interest because security researcher Scott Helme analyzed eMudhra’s certs and found one the private keys it used “is the number 4.” “Not a number that starts with 4, or the number 4 followed by a few hundred random digits, just, 4... Another one is 56, and another is 115. I know, because I recovered all of them from their public certificates on my laptop just now, and it took less than a second,” Helme wrote. Other researchers have found private keys including the numbers 66, 155, 156, 230 and 237. Those are vastly inadequate keys, because they’re easy to guess, making all certs issued by eMudhra susceptible to brute force attacks. As Helme put it: “A P-384 private key should be a random 384-bit number, which gives you 2³⁸⁴ possibilities (or roughly 10¹¹⁵), so nobody is ever going to search that.” This is a developing story and The Register will update it as more information becomes available. ®

item.title: Auto tech startup claims it traced hack attempt back to rival's IP address
item.description: An automotive tech startup claims that its IT systems were attacked by individuals trying to steal its driving model, and that those attacks came from an IP address associated with a rival in the space. The tech startup, IQ.Lvbs, described the alleged security incident in a recent blog post . On October 3, IQ.Lvbs introduced the private beta of NovaSpark , the first model for the company's IQ.Pilot app, in the Comma.ai Discord channel. They put it in that channel because the model requires the use of Comma.ai's camera hardware, which is built for self-driving vehicles. From there, things got weird. "From October 7 to 14, we faced repeated attempts to steal NovaSpark, access users’ devices and private driving files, and exploit our sign-in system," the IQ.Lvbs blog post claims. "The first requests came from an IP assigned to Comma.ai Inc." In addition, on October 8 – shortly after the alleged attacks began – somebody banned IQ.Lvbs' team from the Comma.ai Discord channel. Posts on the IQ.Pilot Discord channel indicate that individuals doing private beta testing for IQ.Lvbs have also been banned from that channel. One of the three people involved in IQ.Lvbs, a UI/UX designer who asked to be identified only as "Cat," speculated to The Register about the reasons for the alleged hack and Discord ban. "Our model, NovaSpark, is a good deal ahead of Comma's latest small and large models, which directly threatens their core business of making AI models good enough to sell their hardware," he said. "Comma for the most part has been stagnant in their models' improvement and that was a main driver for us making NovaSpark." An October 7, 2026 Discord message from user Torq_boi, said to be Harald Schäfer, Comma.ai’s CTO, implies NovaSpark was distilled from Comma.ai's Rebellious Hope model. “I’m glad people are training models and experimenting with this stuff," the post starts. "But don’t lie to people about what you’re doing, and saying it’s not a finetune of existing comma models when it is. That’s not cool.” IQ.Lvbs disputes that assertion and says it did the work on its own. "The claim that NovaSpark is Rebellious Hope with a short fine-tune and an unchanged policy does not survive scrutiny, and we’re not sure how Comma came to that conclusion, especially considering that they do not possess NovaSpark’s model weights or ONNX," the biz said. In the log data IQ.Lvbs published to support its claims, the company flags the username haraschax as one of those associated with Comma.ai IP addresses. Schäfer uses that username on GitHub. Comma.ai and Schäfer did not respond to requests for comment sent to several different addresses. The Discord user Torq_boi in the Comma.ai channel did not respond to a DM seeking comment. Comma.ai is currently being investigated [PDF] by the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration to assess whether its driving automation tech contributed to five crashes and three deaths. item.title: Tens of thousands of Nvidia GPUs sit idle in Meta's Prometheus supercluster, just waiting for a failure
item.description: More than 11 percent of the GPUs at Meta’s Prometheus supercluster in New Albany, Ohio, are either dead or sitting idle waiting to step in when the next drops out, Zuckercorp revealed this week. The massive pool of redundant GPUs is just one of several measures the hyperscaler has taken to keep its AI training runs on track. Prometheus is among Meta's largest compute deployments to date. Powered by Nvidia's Grace Blackwell and (soon) Vera Rubin rack systems, Meta says the supercluster will eventually scale to a gigawatt of capacity spanning about a million accelerators. But as anyone who has worked on a large scale compute cluster understands, whether for LLM training or traditional HPC workloads, more chips inevitably means more problems. In an eight-GPU node, the chance of having a GPU fail is relatively low. In a 100,000-GPU cluster, failures are unavoidable. Meta is building something that's 10x larger and requires distributed training runs across multiple datacenters. Keeping the entire thing humming long enough to reach the next checkpoint becomes a major headache. In a blog post published this week, Meta offered a unique look at the work it's done to keep failures from derailing the development of models like Muse Spark or its most recent release Muse Wonder. Idle GPUs are the cost of continuity When Meta began the first phase of its Prometheus deployment in New Albany, the company says, it was experiencing roughly 1,000 interruptions per day for every 8,000 GPUs. Interruptions don't mean GPU failure. They simply mean something crashed, failed, or timed out, forcing the training run to stop and roll back to the last known good checkpoint. Meta claims in the year since it's been able to cut down the number of interruptions by 99 percent, to about 11 per day per 8,000 GPUs. One of the ways it's done this is by keeping some of Prometheus' GPUs in reserve. The cluster is currently powered by a combination of GB200 and GB300 systems, each with 72 GPUs per NVLink domain. However, only 64 of them are ever in use at any given moment. The other eight are essentially hot spares. Meta did this because a single failed GPU would take out an entire rack and interrupt the training run. Now, when a GPU fails, one of the spares can slot in and take its place. While this saves time — Meta doesn't have to drop the entire rack from the cluster or wait for someone to swap the faulty component to start training again — a failed GPU would still result in an interruption, albeit a shorter one. Parallel resiliency To mitigate this, Meta took advantage of the fact that large scale training jobs usually use data parallelism, where multiple copies of the model are resident within the cluster. "When a fault can be isolated to a data-parallel model replica, we reduce the impact of a hardware failure by allowing a single faulty replica to be taken offline, while the remaining cluster repeats that step and continues productive training," Meta explained. item.content:encoded: More than 11 percent of the GPUs at Meta’s Prometheus supercluster in New Albany, Ohio, are either dead or sitting idle waiting to step in when the next drops out, Zuckercorp revealed this week. The massive pool of redundant GPUs is just one of several measures the hyperscaler has taken to keep its AI training runs on track. Prometheus is among Meta's largest compute deployments to date. Powered by Nvidia's Grace Blackwell and (soon) Vera Rubin rack systems, Meta says the supercluster will eventually scale to a gigawatt of capacity spanning about a million accelerators. But as anyone who has worked on a large scale compute cluster understands, whether for LLM training or traditional HPC workloads, more chips inevitably means more problems. In an eight-GPU node, the chance of having a GPU fail is relatively low. In a 100,000-GPU cluster, failures are unavoidable. Meta is building something that's 10x larger and requires distributed training runs across multiple datacenters. Keeping the entire thing humming long enough to reach the next checkpoint becomes a major headache. In a blog post published this week, Meta offered a unique look at the work it's done to keep failures from derailing the development of models like Muse Spark or its most recent release Muse Wonder. Idle GPUs are the cost of continuity When Meta began the first phase of its Prometheus deployment in New Albany, the company says, it was experiencing roughly 1,000 interruptions per day for every 8,000 GPUs. Interruptions don't mean GPU failure. They simply mean something crashed, failed, or timed out, forcing the training run to stop and roll back to the last known good checkpoint. Meta claims in the year since it's been able to cut down the number of interruptions by 99 percent, to about 11 per day per 8,000 GPUs. One of the ways it's done this is by keeping some of Prometheus' GPUs in reserve. The cluster is currently powered by a combination of GB200 and GB300 systems, each with 72 GPUs per NVLink domain. However, only 64 of them are ever in use at any given moment. The other eight are essentially hot spares. Meta did this because a single failed GPU would take out an entire rack and interrupt the training run. Now, when a GPU fails, one of the spares can slot in and take its place. While this saves time — Meta doesn't have to drop the entire rack from the cluster or wait for someone to swap the faulty component to start training again — a failed GPU would still result in an interruption, albeit a shorter one. Parallel resiliency To mitigate this, Meta took advantage of the fact that large scale training jobs usually use data parallelism, where multiple copies of the model are resident within the cluster. "When a fault can be isolated to a data-parallel model replica, we reduce the impact of a hardware failure by allowing a single faulty replica to be taken offline, while the remaining cluster repeats that step and continues productive training," Meta explained. "The compromised slice simply restarts on available spare hosts and resynchronizes, converting a potential total system halt into a minor, temporary reduction in aggregate throughput." In other words, Meta's training runs only get interrupted if the fault exceeds the data parallel domain. When this happens, the company has implemented a comprehensive checkpointing scheme, which you can think of a bit like auto-save or a revision history. That way if something does fail, Meta doesn't have to start over from scratch. "Our distributed checkpointing architecture asynchronously saves the model state — including gradients and optimizer data — to multi-tier storage," the company wrote. NVLink growing pains Meta says one of the most difficult challenges was making the NVLink fabrics used to connect 72 GPUs behave like one great big accelerator. Earlier H100 and H200-based systems featured just eight GPUs per NVLink domain, which meant the links were far shorter and less numerous. But this functionality was expanded nine-fold with Nvidia's Blackwell generation. "With over 600,000 NVLink connections, even marginal signal degradation triggers frequent NVLink recovery cycles," the company wrote. To overcome this, Meta had to implement a continuous telemetry system and conduct L11 diagnostic burns to isolate weak links before the systems were put into production. Power was another challenge. Ramping up and down tens of thousands of GPUs for a training run can introduce massive spikes in power consumption called transients, which can overwhelm power supply equipment. According to Meta, by focusing on the stability and reliability of its cluster, it was able to achieve more than 85 percent "goodput" — a measure of useful throughput — for pretraining and more than 90 percent for reinforcement learning on its latest model Muse Wonder. The company's ambitions don't stop here. As it works its way toward a million GPUs, Meta hopes to get its interruption rate down to just two per day for every 8,000 GPUs, or about 100,000 GPU-hours mean time between interrupts. ®

item.title: Palo Alto's firewall OS has been under attack from multiple ransomware groups since June
item.description: Multiple ransomware groups, including Qilin and Inc, have been exploiting a high-severity authentication bypass bug in Palo Alto Networks' PAN-OS, with Unit 42 investigating attacks since early June across numerous industries, such as finance, healthcare, and manufacturing. CVE-2026-0257 affects PAN-OS GlobalProtect portals and gateways, potentially allowing attackers to bypass security restrictions and establish an unauthorized VPN connection. The security vendor first disclosed and patched the bug on May 13 and initially assigned it a medium-severity rating, saying it was aware of attempts to exploit it but had not observed any malicious exploitation. That assessment quickly changed, and by the end of the month, Rapid7 researchers said they observed successful exploitation across multiple customer environments dating back to at least May 17. On Monday, Palo Alto Networks’ consulting and incident response biz, Unit 42, said ransomware crews including Qilin and Inc continue to batter the CVE. “Attackers are leveraging this vulnerability to gain an initial foothold into corporate networks, subsequently bypassing multi-factor authentication (MFA) controls to establish a VPN session,” said Andy Piazza, a senior director of threat intelligence at Unit 42. After gaining initial access, the criminals move laterally across the networks using Remote Desktop Protocol and Server Message Block (SMB), dropping additional malware for credential harvesting and data theft before ultimately deploying ransomware, Piazza warned. In its ongoing investigations, Unit 42 has spotted the ransomware criminals infecting “numerous industries, including education, financial services, healthcare, high tech, hospitality, manufacturing, professional and legal services, government, transportation and logistics, utilities and energy, and wholesale and retail." Palo Alto Networks did not respond to The Register ’s inquiries about the attacks, including how many organizations have been infected. Additionally, ReliaQuest intel analysts warned that “multiple threat groups,” including Settra ransomware operators , are also exploiting the bug to gain initial access to corporate networks via unauthorized VPN sessions. “The most significant evolution in tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs) following successful exploitation of CVE-2026-0257 is the direct pivot to the virtualization layer,” Piazza wrote. “In one notable case, attackers moved from the compromised VPN gateway to the vCenter management appliance. From there, they disabled security controls on ESXi hypervisors (execInstalledOnly) and used a custom tool to perform offline credential dumping directly against a domain controller's virtual disk (VMDK).” This allows the miscreants to bypass in-guest endpoint detection and response products, and represents “a highly sophisticated method” of stealing domain-wide credentials, he added. Additionally, ReliaQuest intel analysts warned that “multiple threat groups,” including Settra ransomware operators , are also exploiting the bug to gain initial access to corporate networks via unauthorized VPN sessions. “The most significant evolution in tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs) following successful exploitation of CVE-2026-0257 is the direct pivot to the virtualization layer,” Piazza wrote. “In one notable case, attackers moved from the compromised VPN gateway to the vCenter management appliance. From there, they disabled security controls on ESXi hypervisors (execInstalledOnly) and used a custom tool to perform offline credential dumping directly against a domain controller's virtual disk (VMDK).” This allows the miscreants to bypass in-guest endpoint detection and response products, and represents “a highly sophisticated method” of stealing domain-wide credentials, he added. Unit 42 has also spotted criminals chaining this exploit for initial access with other vulnerabilities such as CVE-2023-27532 , which targets Veeam backup infrastructure. So if you haven’t already patched vulnerable PAN-OS software, do so now - and investigate whether attackers have already gained access to your network. Check Unit 42’s indicators of compromise to assist with threat-hunting activities.®

item.title: Swamped curl maintainers take low-level flaws public to survive vulnerability 'avalanche'
item.description: An "avalanche of vulnerability reports" is forcing curl to move lower-severity cases into public view, reserving private handling for high and critical flaws. From October 26, low and medium-severity reports should be filed in the open source data transfer tool's public GitHub repository, maintainer Daniel Stenberg said . "Security researchers in doubt can still submit the issue on HackerOne and we can tell them what severity we deem it to be. Over the last few years, over 90 percent of all submissions could quickly be assessed to be less than HIGH." Stenberg already shuttered curl's bug bounty scheme this year as AI-generated submissions piled work onto its security team. Stenberg has previously acknowledged that not all AI-assisted reports are bad, but the workload now demands another response. "This policy change is entirely triggered by the current avalanche of vulnerability reports that keep pouring in . We see no end to them and we do not anticipate this flood to decrease within the next several months. "We are struggling as a project as all key maintainers feel strained, overloaded and brought to the brink of what we can muster. We must act to survive. This is our next step in a survival strategy. It might not be our last. We aim to not drown." Public handling would let more people assess reports, develop fixes, write advisories, and check for related problems before releases ship, Stenberg said. Handling vulnerability reports publicly won't reduce the work per report, he admits, though it could spread the load and make the resulting lessons and documentation easier to find. At least that's the theory. Public disclosure also gives attackers more time to exploit flaws before fixes arrive. The maintainer agrees this is unfortunate yet unavoidable. "We limit this practice to less than HIGH for this reason: at least these problems are not terrible." Stenberg said researchers using AI are generating unusual option combinations unlikely to occur in real applications, then treating minor discrepancies as vulnerabilities. "We can't continue down this spiraling path with our sanity intact. We don't have the bandwidth, manpower or even will to handle a never-ending vulnerability reporting stream at this pace. I believe few software projects can stand this kind of prolonged high volume deluge for extended periods. Something needs to give way." ®

item.title: OneDrive loses bunch of Copilot shortcuts in File Explorer clear-out
item.description: Microsoft is pruning OneDrive's Copilot options from File Explorer's right-click menu, though the AI assistant isn't being shown the door entirely. The Windows giant will remove shortcuts for summarizing documents, generating FAQs, comparing files and images, explaining images, extracting text, and asking questions. The rollout begins in mid-November and is expected to finish by early December. "Ask Copilot" will remain. Microsoft's September 2025 announcement of the feature said: "We are bringing the power of AI directly into your daily file management experience. With just a few clicks, Copilot can help you summarize lengthy documents, generate an FAQ, compare files, or answer questions about your file." Users can still right-click a OneDrive file and select "Ask Copilot" to start a conversation with the file attached, or use the Copilot icon in File Explorer Home. The individual actions will also remain available in the OneDrive activity center. Adding a clutch of Copilot options with identical icons did little to make an already crowded menu easier to navigate. In its message on the subject, Microsoft said: "We're simplifying how people use Copilot with their OneDrive files in File Explorer." An extra click, yes, but at least you won't need a taller screen to view even more context menu options. Microsoft has stated that it intends to adopt a more thoughtful approach to how and where its AI assistant turns up in its product line. In March 2026, Windows boss Pavan Davuluri said : "We are reducing unnecessary Copilot entry points." File Explorer's crowded right-click menu seems as good a place to start as any. The File Explorer context menu is also undergoing an overhaul as part of Microsoft's attempt to make it less "cluttered and sluggish," to the point where users could opt to have it work a bit like it used to in Windows 10. ®

item.title: openEuler brings China's enterprise Linux ambitions to the desktop
item.description: Surprisingly few organizations were promoting Linux distros at Open Source Summit Europe. The only dedicated stands we found belonged to two Chinese projects, with openEuler occupying the larger booth. For users accustomed to Western enterprise distros, openEuler may be a less familiar name, but it has an impressive history. It's the modern free community version of Huawei's EulerOS, a version of which achieved official official UNIX™ certification . openEuler is no longer a solely Huawei project, though. Since then, it's been opened up, and it is now run by the OpenAtom Foundation . OpenAtom was co-founded in 2020 by Huawei along with some other big Chinese names, such as Alibaba, Baidu, and Tencent. Another of the co-founders was Inspur, which formerly developed its own distro, K/UX – a version of which also achieved official UNIX™ certification . Inspur K/UX won Unix certification in February 2016, and EulerOS seven months later. K/UX's Unix certification expired in 2019. A few months later, in May 2019, the US placed wider sanctions on Huawei . It is possible that the fresh restrictions on American sales prompted Huawei's interest in closer co-operation with other companies in the Chinese Linux space. As far as we can see, there were no further versions of K/UX after version 3. As additional motivation for cooperation, both EulerOS and K/UX were originally based on CentOS Linux, and of course, in December 2020, the CentOS Project announced it would shift its focus from CentOS Linux to CentOS Stream . The openEuler community has taken the platform in new directions. It has built its own stack of tools for developing, deploying, and running LLMs, called Intelligence BooM . It has a tool for migrating CentOS Linux systems to openEuler, called x2openEuler . As you would expect, it supports Kubernetes, as well as Docker and Podman, but it also has its own container engine called iSula (named after a species of ant ). Aware that it's less known outside Asia, at the Open Source Summit, OpenAtom was handing out copies of a special "Focus Guide" from Admin Magazine, which is also available as a free download . Some parts of this are also available online without registration, such as AI and the BooM Stack and Automating Migration to openEuler . openEuler has a dual-strand release cycle , akin to Ubuntu rather than the RHELatives, with LTS versions and more frequent "innovation releases." The current LTS is version 24.03, released in June 2024 , while the latest version is 26.09. There is a plethora of versions and editions available on the downloads page : the latest release is for x86-64 and 64-bit Arm. The LTS version adds support for RISC-V and LoongArch, and there are minimal versions for 32-bit Arm as well. The older 22.03 LTS was also available for SW-64, meaning the SunWay RISC processors that Register sister site The Next Platform looked at in 2016. item.dc:creator: Liam Proven
item.content:encoded: Surprisingly few organizations were promoting Linux distros at Open Source Summit Europe. The only dedicated stands we found belonged to two Chinese projects, with openEuler occupying the larger booth. For users accustomed to Western enterprise distros, openEuler may be a less familiar name, but it has an impressive history. It's the modern free community version of Huawei's EulerOS, a version of which achieved official official UNIX™ certification . openEuler is no longer a solely Huawei project, though. Since then, it's been opened up, and it is now run by the OpenAtom Foundation . OpenAtom was co-founded in 2020 by Huawei along with some other big Chinese names, such as Alibaba, Baidu, and Tencent. Another of the co-founders was Inspur, which formerly developed its own distro, K/UX – a version of which also achieved official UNIX™ certification . Inspur K/UX won Unix certification in February 2016, and EulerOS seven months later. K/UX's Unix certification expired in 2019. A few months later, in May 2019, the US placed wider sanctions on Huawei . It is possible that the fresh restrictions on American sales prompted Huawei's interest in closer co-operation with other companies in the Chinese Linux space. As far as we can see, there were no further versions of K/UX after version 3. As additional motivation for cooperation, both EulerOS and K/UX were originally based on CentOS Linux, and of course, in December 2020, the CentOS Project announced it would shift its focus from CentOS Linux to CentOS Stream . The openEuler community has taken the platform in new directions. It has built its own stack of tools for developing, deploying, and running LLMs, called Intelligence BooM . It has a tool for migrating CentOS Linux systems to openEuler, called x2openEuler . As you would expect, it supports Kubernetes, as well as Docker and Podman, but it also has its own container engine called iSula (named after a species of ant ). Aware that it's less known outside Asia, at the Open Source Summit, OpenAtom was handing out copies of a special "Focus Guide" from Admin Magazine, which is also available as a free download . Some parts of this are also available online without registration, such as AI and the BooM Stack and Automating Migration to openEuler . openEuler has a dual-strand release cycle , akin to Ubuntu rather than the RHELatives, with LTS versions and more frequent "innovation releases." The current LTS is version 24.03, released in June 2024 , while the latest version is 26.09. There is a plethora of versions and editions available on the downloads page : the latest release is for x86-64 and 64-bit Arm. The LTS version adds support for RISC-V and LoongArch, and there are minimal versions for 32-bit Arm as well. The older 22.03 LTS was also available for SW-64, meaning the SunWay RISC processors that Register sister site The Next Platform looked at in 2016. As LWN put it last year , this is a "non-upstream kernel port." There are five types of installation ISO available: Offline Standard, Offline Everything (a hefty 24.9 GB), Network Install (a still significant 1.5 GB), and two variants of the desktop "DevStation" version – a basic one at 3.3 GB and an "everything" edition at 25 GB. We gave the DevStation a very quick whirl in VirtualBox. It boots into its own installation program called Heolleo , which offers the choice of Simplified Chinese or English. Installation took a while, as it automatically fetches updates as it goes. We ended up with a GNOME desktop configured for Chinese, but we opened Settings, typed "language" into the Search box, and picked English. After a reboot, we could read most of the desktop. Program groups and some other elements are still in Chinese, but it's navigable with a bit of guesswork. It's GNOME 49, with the Dash to Panel and Arc Menu extensions preinstalled for a slightly more familiar layout. Opening a terminal, we were greeted with: Welcome to 6.18.48-0.0.0.15.oe2609.x86_64 It also offers the Deepin Desktop Environment, UKUI (as seen in Ubuntu Kylin), MATE, Xfce, and the Kiran Desktop Environment , which is a new one to us. In places, the English-language materials for openEuler mention Chinese CPU makers rather than western ones – which is understandable, in context. Examples include processors from Hygon, a Chinese licensee of AMD designs , as well as Phytium and Kunpeng , which explain the Arm support on offer. In the western world, the Red Hat user community responded to the end of CentOS Linux by building new free distros that stay as close as they can to their progenitor: the Rocky Linux and AlmaLinux projects , rebuilt from Red Hat source code. Then, when the IBM subsidiary restricted access to that source to its customers in 2023, the Rocky and AlmaLinux projects started to diverge. Rocky aims for the closest possible RHEL compatibility, and its most visible innovation is that it's built its own new build service . It also found a clever workaround to get Red Hat's kernel source code. AlmaLinux still targets RHEL compatibility, but differentiates itself by retaining older device support and older CPU architectures after Red Hat drops them. Chinese vendors have responded very differently. Those offering CentOS Linux-based OSes clubbed together, dropped their rival versions and their UNIX compatibility efforts, and instead are working on new tools and subsystems. Much like European interest in digital sovereignty , this is in part due to the Trump administration. Half a decade after it was cut off from its upstream sources, the openEuler platform is thriving and growing, even if few in the western world pay any attention at all. ®

item.title: How going dual-native means VM/container co-existence and sovereign security in the AI era
item.description: Seasoned techies recall with nostalgia a simpler time when the “single-stack” model of enterprise computing held as the default approach to solving interoperability headaches. Back then IT decision-makers were prepared to forfeit some choice and flexibility in how they specified IT systems in return for the availability and manageability that came with a homogenous operating environment. With the subsequent rise of multi-clouds, application-specific hardware, ever-changing business requirements, and the race for AI, the old “one-size-fits-all” playbook has been largely abandoned. Most IT estates have embraced technological diversity, some by design, some through standardization, some by inertia. Modern enterprise environments have become innately heterogeneous – and innately complex. They run a diverse combo of system software, hardware devices, cloud services, legacy applications, et al . The advance of AI has brought standard CPUs, specialized GPUs, fast networking fabrics, distributed data pipelines, and new deployment models that span private clouds, public clouds, edge – and ever-pressing ROI expectations. But that doesn’t mean that companies’ existing applications and data simply disappear. One trying but inevitable outcome of rapid AI deployment is the so-called “VM-container divide”. This is where critical business applications tipped to transition to containers continue to run on virtual machines, because cloud-native services are taking precedence, nabbing container and Kubernetes availability. So companies face the challenge of operationalizing AI, without being forced into complex migrations or creating new infrastructure silos. Dealing with this technological schism poses acute challenges for IT management. Many new AI deployments are going straight to containers, while existing data and applications – which the AI needs to access – continue to run on VMs. Running separate stacks for VMs and containers creates a number of issues, such as duplicate capacity plans, separate support contracts, and fragmented governance. And after years of trying to get beyond the pitfalls of siloed data, exasperated enterprises are now having to deal with siloed infrastructure. Separately managed VM and container environments often mean inefficient resource utilization. This in turn can lead to “stranded capacity” – installed computing resources that cannot be used to support live workloads. VM clusters are frequently underutilized while container pools (like Kubernetes) are overprovisioned, with no easy way to share resources without manual intervention. Furthermore, VM/container infrastructure fragmentation can create an operations bottleneck for agentic AI. Infrastructure fragmentation can complicate the deployment, integration, governance, and scaling of agents thus making it harder to operationalize and scale agentic AI securely and consistently. item.dc:creator: James Hayes
item.content:encoded: Seasoned techies recall with nostalgia a simpler time when the “single-stack” model of enterprise computing held as the default approach to solving interoperability headaches. Back then IT decision-makers were prepared to forfeit some choice and flexibility in how they specified IT systems in return for the availability and manageability that came with a homogenous operating environment. With the subsequent rise of multi-clouds, application-specific hardware, ever-changing business requirements, and the race for AI, the old “one-size-fits-all” playbook has been largely abandoned. Most IT estates have embraced technological diversity, some by design, some through standardization, some by inertia. Modern enterprise environments have become innately heterogeneous – and innately complex. They run a diverse combo of system software, hardware devices, cloud services, legacy applications, et al . The advance of AI has brought standard CPUs, specialized GPUs, fast networking fabrics, distributed data pipelines, and new deployment models that span private clouds, public clouds, edge – and ever-pressing ROI expectations. But that doesn’t mean that companies’ existing applications and data simply disappear. One trying but inevitable outcome of rapid AI deployment is the so-called “VM-container divide”. This is where critical business applications tipped to transition to containers continue to run on virtual machines, because cloud-native services are taking precedence, nabbing container and Kubernetes availability. So companies face the challenge of operationalizing AI, without being forced into complex migrations or creating new infrastructure silos. Dealing with this technological schism poses acute challenges for IT management. Many new AI deployments are going straight to containers, while existing data and applications – which the AI needs to access – continue to run on VMs. Running separate stacks for VMs and containers creates a number of issues, such as duplicate capacity plans, separate support contracts, and fragmented governance. And after years of trying to get beyond the pitfalls of siloed data, exasperated enterprises are now having to deal with siloed infrastructure. Separately managed VM and container environments often mean inefficient resource utilization. This in turn can lead to “stranded capacity” – installed computing resources that cannot be used to support live workloads. VM clusters are frequently underutilized while container pools (like Kubernetes) are overprovisioned, with no easy way to share resources without manual intervention. Furthermore, VM/container infrastructure fragmentation can create an operations bottleneck for agentic AI. Infrastructure fragmentation can complicate the deployment, integration, governance, and scaling of agents thus making it harder to operationalize and scale agentic AI securely and consistently. When AI agents cannot autonomously communicate across environments, their utility droops from autonomous problem-solvers to plain localised macros. Containers are gaining because of the widespread embrace of AI-enabled applications. Eighty-five percent of IT executives polled by Nutanix’s most recent Enterprise Cloud Index survey think that AI is accelerating their organization’s adoption of containers in a meaningful way; 29 percent think it is speeding-up adoption “to a great extent”. “AI is accelerating the shift to containers because machine learning models require strict dependency packing, while critical applications and data remain spread across both virtualised and containerised environments,” says Harsha Kotikela, Senior Director of Product & Solutions Marketing at Nutanix. Agents are multi-tier by nature he explains. “Inference is typically GPU-intensive and container-based, while agents are often CPU-intensive and container-based, and existing enterprise applications and data largely remain in VM environments. The challenge is to bring these tiers together so agents can work with enterprise applications and data, without forcing migration or creating additional infrastructure silos.” The application landscape, meanwhile, has become just as diverse. Many organisations simultaneously operate traditional enterprise applications running on VMs, containerised apps, distributed AI applications and intelligent agents, with workloads deployed across private cloud, public cloud, and edge. Each environment has its own management tools, operational processes, security rules and governance models. “Management capability has struggled to scale up commensurately,” says Kotikela, but adding more consoles or building separate operational teams for every technology stack does not necessarily solve this complexity: “In many cases, it increases it.” However, Kotikela challenges the notion that the predicament enterprises face in straddling the VM-container divide is intractable. Rather, the challenge is to move towards a unified operating model that allows them to operationalize agentic AI while retaining flexibility across their existing and new environments. “Rather than trying to work around heterogeneity, the objective now should be to make heterogeneous environments operate consistently with purposeful policies,” Kotikela says. “This is where Nutanix's dual-native architecture comes in, enabling enterprises to operationalize agentic AI across container-based inference and agent workloads alongside existing VM-based applications and data, through a consistent operating model.” The reality is that the VM-to-container migration trend is sluggish, Kotikela suggests. Few enterprises are starting from scratch with containers. Many have long-established business applications on legacy architectures, on top of which they are building container-based applications, but mostly not to replace what they already have running on VMs. Rather, they are prolonging their VM investment. It’s customer interest that’s informed how Nutanix provisions a governed, dual-native architecture through its Nutanix Cloud Platform – NCP – which runs traditional VMs and containerised/Kubernetes-based AI workloads concurrently on a single, consistent infrastructure. NCP’s hybrid-cloud infrastructure foundation unifies compute, storage, virtualisation and management across on-premises resources, public clouds and edge. It works in concert with Nutanix Enterprise AI (NAI), which provides the software capabilities to deploy, govern, and scale AI workloads. Technology partnerships are vital to building AI support functionality into Nutanix's AI portfolio, explains Kotikela. “Nutanix and NVIDIA work together to provide an integrated platform for enterprise AI, combining Nutanix’s hybrid-cloud infrastructure and software with NVIDIA’s accelerated computing and AI software. Nutanix Enterprise AI simplifies the deployment, management, and secure operation of AI models, integrating with NVIDIA NIM and NeMo microservices to support enterprise AI inference and agentic AI workflows.” Meanwhile, “Nutanix Kubernetes Platform provides the foundation for managing Kubernetes environments, while Nutanix Unified Storage delivers the high-performance data access required by AI workloads. Together, these capabilities help enterprises deploy and scale AI while maintaining control over their infrastructure, models, and data.” Stacks of opportunity “In an ideal IT world you do not want to have to manage two different operational stacks – but the world of IT is rarely ‘ideal’,” Kotikela points out. “So you have to approach the challenge from a realistic perspective. You cannot bend your current stacks to a different reality without the risk of something breaking, and there’s no sense in that.” He adds: “A platform that unifies VMs and containers improves developer time-to-value by getting rid of those infrastructure silos, and providing a single control plane.” Rather than development teams having to manage separate pipelines for existing VMs and

item.title: The dangers of letting tech billionaires shape our world
item.description: As SpaceX impacts Ukraine and AI-generated music divides artists and fans, critics are asking what happens when technology has too much control over our lives This was originally published in TechScape, a newsletter about how technology shapes our lives. Sign up to receive it here Hello, and welcome to TechScape. I’m Blake Montgomery, US tech editor at the Guardian, writing to you while sitting in front of Roy Lichtenstein’s monumental Drowning Girl, on view in New York City . Today in tech, we’re discussing the perils of Elon Musk’s one-man global infrastructure, AI-generated music and a Guardian AI conference in Paris. Continue reading...

item.title: Labor and the Coalition are poised to take a reckless gamble on AI. Haven’t they realised community support has collapsed? | Edward Santow and Sarah Sacher
item.description: Australian workers expect the government to act to protect them from AI harms. There is a clear reform solution at hand Get our new political email , free app or daily news podcast Australia’s major political parties are edging towards rare consensus. Labor and the Coalition increasingly want to take a major bet on artificial intelligence. Yet, just as the parties are coming together, the Australian community is running the other way. Last year, only 30% of Australians believed the benefits of AI outweighed the risks. In 2026, community trust in AI appears to be falling even further. Continue reading...

item.title: I’m a CTO. AI still needs your human expertise | Madhu Shashanka
item.description: AI is increasingly getting good at doing some tasks, but it can never replace human workers’ judgment Autonomous cars, which may be the safest we have built, keep getting easily avoidable parking tickets. While Waymos crash far less often than human drivers over tens of millions of miles, they’re still terrible at performing basic tasks – keeping out of disabled parking spots and tow-away zones, or steering clear of a church garage during Sunday service, according to the Wall Street Journal . That is the state of AI today: impressively capable at something complex, yet embarrassingly clumsy at something easy. And it has implications for what work will remain human and what will be automated by AI. Madhu Shashanka is co-founder, chief scientist and chief technology officer at Concentric AI, a data security software company Continue reading...

item.title: Googlebook review: Google’s new laptops are woefully underbaked
item.description: Great hardware let down by software flaws on these pricey machines that combine ChromeOS with Android Google’s attempt to create a new type of laptop to compete with Windows and macOS machines is finally here, combining the best of ChromeOS and Android into the new Googlebook. With advanced links to Android phones and the best of Google built in, can these Googlebooks really compete with a MacBook Air or Surface Laptop? I took two for a spin to find out. For years, Chromebooks have been the boss of budget laptops, but Googlebooks take a different, far more premium approach. Made by a range of traditional PC makers, including Acer, Asus, Dell, HP and Lenovo, they start at £999 (€1,099/ $899 / A$2,299 ) – a far cry from the £160 Chromebooks. Continue reading...

item.title: Wikipedia often gets taken for granted – but its history is fascinating, and its future is fragile
item.description: Wikipedia’s 68m articles have been consulted trillions of times. Not bad for a website that has barely changed since it was founded 20 years ago A few years ago, I was struck by the tension between how Wikipedia was used, and how it was talked about. Everyone was on it all the time, and yet its reputation had stalled at “don’t trust it”, because it was the “free encyclopedia that anyone can edit”. Clearly people were trusting it, so much so it had become part of the fabric of everyday life since it was founded by Jimmy Wales and Larry Sanger in 2001. But despite the fact it now has been consulted trillions of times by billions of people (English Wikipedia alone is 5.2bn words long), it inspires an odd lack of curiosity. Even people donating to Wikipedia might say the money was “for the factcheckers”, though there aren’t any – not paid ones, anyway. Meanwhile, the internet in the social media era had begun to feel like a much uglier place, and some digital nostalgia was setting in: here was this holdover that had somehow survived; a website that functions – and even looks – much the same as it did 20 years ago. Continue reading...

item.title: Penguin Colony review – an Antarctic odyssey of Nazis and Lovecraftian horrors
item.description: PC; Origame Digital This odd but absorbing adventure sends you waddling across Antarctica in search of an eldritch entity – uncovering a world far stranger than it first appears A Nazi kneels down on frozen snow, staring at an endless Antarctic horizon. Another holds a gun to his head, ready to end his own life. I direct a small waddling penguin up to them, trying to imagine what it could be thinking. Dismay, perhaps. Likely bewilderment. But then a faint smile seems to break out across its beaky face, as if amused by these silly humans and their misguided belief that they could ever best this howling, harsh landscape. For most games, the idea of playing as a penguin observing Nazis losing the plot near the south pole would be weird enough. But Penguin Colony, developed by Origame Digital, pushes further. This is an audacious, frequently brilliant retelling of HP Lovecraft’s 1936 novella At the Mountains of Madness, in which eldritch horrors are just as common as Nazis. Further weirdness abounds: the many collectibles scattered about this place are not shiny gold objects à la Super Mario or Sonic. Rather, they are words. So tottering about as a semiaquatic bird, you have a unique mission: collect human language. Continue reading...

item.title: From Mario to machine guns: how Ubisoft Paris made Tom Clancy’s Rainbow Six Tactics
item.description: The studio is swapping the Mushroom Kingdom’s vivid palette for the blood-soaked grit of military action series Where do you go after Mario? It’s a question the team at Ubisoft Paris found itself pondering three years ago after wrapping up work on the charming turn-based tactics adventure, Mario + Rabbids: Sparks of Hope , sequel to its unexpected crossover hit, Mario + Rabbids: Kingdom Battle. By melding a rather specialist genre with video gaming’s biggest household name, the developer introduced chin-stroking strategic play to a whole new audience. “ Having the opportunity to work with the Mario franchise was a privilege, and it’s still something I’m very proud of,” says level designer director, Julien Vial. “I still remember seeing the first prototype and being blown away by all the possibilities . ” Now, Ubisoft Paris has returned with a new project, but this time the studio is swapping the Mushroom Kingdom’s vivid palette for the blood-soaked grit of military action series Rainbow Six. Where Mario and Rabbids saw squishy creatures bounce harmlessly across levels as Mario encased foes in honey, Rainbow Six Tactics, a turn-based tactical spin-off from Rainbow Six Siege , sees balaclava-clad insurgents take shrapnel rounds to the chest. A seamless tonal shift, then. Continue reading...

item.title: Companies rushed in on AI. Now some are pulling back
item.description: Rapid AI adoption left workers cleaning up a flood of errors and low-quality work Employers around the globe are grappling with the fallout from rushing to adopt fast-changing artificial intelligence tools. Meta has scaled back plans to axe staff and use more AI agents after the company found employees were spending more and more time cleaning up technical and security errors, Reuters reported . And after thinning its workforce, especially middle managers , in a 2023 efficiency push, the company is expanding its managerial ranks again, LinkedIn posts from workers show. Continue reading...

The AirPods 5 have the same design the popular AirPods 4 offering an option for those that do not like silicone ear tips used by most noise cancelling earbuds. They come in two versions, with or without a wireless charging case and swipe controls, costing from £119 (€149/$129/A$219) – £10 cheaper than the launch price of their predecessors . item.title: Systolic style: meet the medical-grade smartwatch revolutionising blood pressure monitoring
item.description: An estimated one-third of adults in England have high blood pressure, with research showing that many are unaware of their condition. But thanks to the new Huawei Watch D3, monitoring blood pressure is easier, accurate and more stylish than ever Wearable technology has come a long way in the past decade. Take a look around at your colleagues, friends and family, and you’ll be hard pushed to find anyone not wearing some kind of health monitoring ring, watch or band – there are even tracking insoles and patches, too. These gadgets have myriad benefits – not least, allowing us more control and insight over our health and wellbeing than ever before. We’re able to monitor everything from sleep and stress to heart health and more, and the technology is becoming more refined and intuitive seemingly by the day. Continue reading...

item.title: Intuitive living is the latest wellness trend – meet the new tech making it work
item.description: Wellness culture can be overwhelming, but a more fluid approach is emerging. Smart devices such as the Huawei Watch Fit 5 perfectly embody this shift in direction – whether you’re regularly sleep tracking or just occasionally using data to support your lifestyle When it comes to the world of health and wellness, it’s easy to suffer from information overwhelm. We’ve never had more access to data, research and expertise which, while valuable, isn’t always applicable to our own lives. What’s more, few of us have time to spend hours sifting through content to devise a personalised health routine, let alone work out if a “routine” is necessary at all. All this information and expectation can come at a cost: emotional strain, guilt and confusion about where to turn. Health and fitness then start to feel like abstract milestones that we’re blindly chasing rather than important components of our lives. Continue reading...

item.title: The story of ‘earvolution’: from ceremonial piercings to fashion-statement earbuds
item.description: For millennia, humans have been captivated by ear decorations. Now, earbuds not only connect us to the digital world, they also showcase our personal sense of style – and the HUAWEI FreeClip 2 is at the forefront of that development When we are born, a cry can let the world know that we are healthy and OK. When we first begin to talk, we learn to express our needs and understand the needs of others. As we grow older, we learn that the sound of a siren denotes danger, that certain notes swelling together create the sound of a favourite song which lifts our spirits, or that a warm familiar voice on the other end of the phone means our best friend has our back. Our ears give us grounding and clues: they are our maps of the world, guiding us towards truth, keeping us from harm, giving us a constant stream of sensory information. Continue reading...
